There was something almost cinematic about it - driving down the highway as monetary policy was being reset on a meeting-by-meeting rhythm. The one- and three-month €STR futures express views on or hedge exposure to the ECB policy rate. Each contract trades until the end of the 1-month (1m) or 3-month (3m) period that starts in the contract month. For example, the last trading date of the Jun-26 3m €STR contract is 15-Sep-26. This is because the underlying is the average €STR rate accrued over the 3m period ending 1 business day prior to the 3rd Wednesday of the 3rd calendar month after the start of the accrual period. records.text: MEA EM, CEE shows the clearest signs of refla- tion. CEE credit growth is strong across the board for households and corporates. The pickup in corporate credit is typically FX positive given that it reflects investment cycles underway. Private consumption is still the main driver of CEE growth, aided by the transmission of previous policy rate cuts and positive wealth effects as CEE house prices con- tinue to surge, but we think more “resilient” CEE growth sources will keep gaining prominence. There are tentative signs of that in industrial production. Looking ahead, the drawdown and disbursement of EU funds should boost CEE capex (Figure 3C E E c a p e x c y c l e t o g e t f u r t h e r b o o s t ) and growth, particularly for Hungary as large EU funds get unlocked. So far, this positive growth environment has not driven CEE inflation sharply higher, but averages are flattered by Hungary and headline inflation is flattered by fiscal intervention. Yet inflation momentum still lingers above target, which, given the upside inflation risks down the line, does not suggest a goldilocks environment where CEE central banks can cut through strong growth and stable currencies. That could well narrow the forecasted baseload supply-demand gap due to slow buildout of gas turbines. However, solar-BESS ramping will remain challenging in markets with less favourable conditions, in our view. Regional preferences: Among major US power markets, we think California’s sunny weather, high gas prices and carbon tax make it ideal to build co-located solar and BESS as an alternative to gas for baseload power. For Texas and Southwest, low gas prices may make it more economical to build gas turbines, but strong sunlight and current difficulties with turbine procurement continue to incentivise solar–BESS builds in the pipeline . We expect PJM – which serves 13 eastern states and is the largest data centre market in the US – to continue relying on gas for baseload power due to the region’s relativelylow and variable levels of sunlight . Europe generally sees high costs of gas generation due to the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) and reliance on imported gas, making a strong case for renewables. Spain and Germany stand out as highly competitive, though lower sunlight hours in Germany would see higher costs due to oversizing. We note that investors appear to be sceptical of Burnham’s policy stance, but unless we see a sharp turn there (or closer to the budget) then GBP carry, positioning and UK resilience could frustrate sterling shorts (strong UK retail sales today and new high in retail sales volumes since 2022, with potential PMI bounce next week and GBP still high on our quant rankings). As markets get closer to the Autumn Budget and/or a shift in policy messaging from a less market friendly PM candi- date such as Andy Burnham then yes, fiscal concerns could finally weaken GBP. However, there could well be a prolonged period before that where markets are frustrated and find it harder to greatly increase fiscal risk premium in GBP. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 13 Market-Implied | # of Months to Next Central Bank Move Months to Next Hike/Cut measures the market-implied time until the next expected central bank policy move. By using market forward pricing, it estimates the number of months until policy shifts occur. It reflects how traders interpret near-term conditions and serves as a useful signal of expected central bank timing. This provides investors with a granular view of when policy changes are anticipated and how these expectations evolve over time. Use cases The primary use case of these tickers is to provide investors with a market‑implied estimate of the number of months until the next expected central bank rate hike or cut. This granularity allows markets to anticipate policy changes even before official meeting dates. Additionally, researchers can overlay the series with macro variables (e.g., inflation surprises, employment data) to study how efficiently markets incorporate new information into policy rate expectations over time. When combined with the companion pace tickers and terminal rate measures, they form a comprehensive framework for understanding both the direction and timing of monetary policy cycles. Calculation methodology We first compute the trough/peak using the methodology mentioned in the Market- Implied | Peak/Trough Central Bank Policy Rates, with the only difference being that the time horizon is limited to 5 years instead of 30 years. Growth trajectories, labour‑market dynamics, productivity potential and the inflation path are central to the cross‑asset narrative, especially as the new Fed Chair’s emphasis on AI‑driven disinflation has intensified the internal debate about how AI could reshape wages, prices and the policy reaction functions. At the risk of oversimplification, the two broad narratives that coexist today are a) AI is driving rates higher in the short term by strong demand to build computing power and data centers, especially in an economy already near full capacity, and in the long run by increasing the expected real rate of return through productivity enhancement; b) AI productivity gains are deeply disinflationary in the medium term, allowing the economy to deliver strong real rates of return without pressuring the labour market, leaving room for easier monetary policy. We compared today's narratives to those of the mid-to-late 1990s to identify where the current cycle resembles that period and where it differs. The 1996–97 period offers a useful template for thinking about how markets can trade ahead of hard productivity proof. At the time, equities were entering an earnings multiple‑driven rerating, as markets priced a step-up in trend growth from corporate IT capex. The MPC at large continued with its approach of an 'active hold' heading into summer – and for good reason. Four things stood out to us in the minutes, marking a clear departure from the April decision. First, risk of second-round effects have subtly changed. In April, the MPC noted that there was "a risk of material second-round effects in price and wage-setting, which policy would need to lean against". In June, this was softened to a more conditional statement: the "risk of material second-round effects in price and wage- setting, against which policy needs to lean, is greater the longer higher energy prices persist". This, in our view, marked a subtle but important shift in risk assessment for the broader committee. Second, financial conditions are still doing some of the work for the MPC – consistent with the 'active hold' strategy. In fact, the MPC noted that there "had been full and fast pass-through from increases in such rates to key lending rates for household and businesses" – with most members judging that "this tightening provided insurance against inflation risks, while preserving optionality to adjust course as more conclusive evidence emerged". records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 319/06/2026 Fiscal pressures in 2026: Chile’s public accounts face pressure from a weaker-than-expected economy reducing tax revenues, higher energy-stabilization spending, and ambitious reform commitments that require congressional approval in an unfavourable legislative environment. Wider deficit than anticipated: In our base case, we expect the 2026 fiscal deficit at 2.5% of GDP. We think the widening will be driven by a revenue shortfall due to lower-than-budgeted activity (~0.3pp of GDP), higher energy-stabilization costs (~0.2pp) and increased spending on health, housing and social programs. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz has publicly stated that the Kast administration has inherited a bigger fiscal challenge than anticipated, alleging revenue overestimation and undisclosed expenditure commitments from the previous government. This scenario requires congressional authorization for debt issuance beyond planned levels. The USD6.2bn requirement: The government has announced total financing requirements of roughly USD6.2bn for 2026, a sizable increase from previous years. The planned mix is about 70% domestic (CLP-denominated) and 30% external (USD-denominated) debt. What will drive FX returns in 2H26 through the lens of systematic models? Carry should continue to drive FX returns in 2H amid constructive risk sentiment, recovering growth and elevat- ed yield gaps given sticky inflation. Going into this year, we anticipated a lower level of central bank activity, favouring carry and relative commodity momentum strategies. These 2 themes have played out, but were driven by a totally different backdrop. 1H26 has been marked by (i) renewed inflationary concerns on the back of elevated oil prices and (ii) resilience in risk assets driven by the strong performance of the AI equity complex. In this renewed inflationary backdrop, notably the returns of our real carry basket have been twice as large as the nominal/risk-ad- justed implementation for the Global/EM portfolios, as dis- cussed above. records.text: Warsh introduced a task force that would look into: 1) Fed communications, 2) the Fed’s balance sheet policy, 3) the use and reliance on existing data sources, 4) productivity and jobs in an era of transformation, and 5) the Fed’s inflation frameworks. In response to the hawkish-toned messaging, 2Y Treasury yields closed 11bp higher on the day, the UST curve broadly flattened and OIS forward markets are now pricing in a full hike by October and ~47bp of cumulative hikes by April 2027. Importantly, reduced forward guidance could put additional weight on speeches by FOMC officials (regional Fed presidents in particular) and may lead to more volatility and event risk, increasing term premiums and nominal yields. Consequently, we think yields are biased higher and, even with the latest move, we believe that the 10s/30s curve is still too steep and recommend holding 10s/30s UST flatteners. We expect the Fed to stay behind the curve, i.e. delivering enough hawkishness to support credibility, potentially even hiking before year-end but still endorsing a modest and gradual adjustment to policy rates with limited damage to risk assets. Our baseline call is for patience and a first hike in 2H27 but believe the margin for error and the tolerance for further inflation is limited, with genuine risks of earlier hikes. records.text: France—Early Thoughts on the 2027 Elections We provide early thoughts on the 2027 elections in France and their potential implications for the economic and fiscal outlook. An Open Race for President French voters will elect their next President in a little less than a year, with the first round of the elections taking place in April 2027.1 The outcome of the elections looks highly uncertain, since incumbent President Macron is prevented by the Constitution from standing for a third consecutive term. There are already 25 declared candidates, with recent additions including former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal in the centre and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. More candidates—such as Raphaël Glucksmann on the centre-left—are likely to announce their bid over coming months. The far-right Rassemblement National will also formalise Jordan Bardella’s candidacy if Marine Le Pen remains under an electoral ban after the verdict of her appeal trial on July 7. The number of presidential hopefuls is then likely to narrow ahead of the elections, with some press reports suggesting that former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe on the centre-right and Attal could agree on a single candidacy. First-round polls show Rassemblement National claiming around 30-35% of votes, well ahead of anyone else, making their candidate very likely to advance to the second round (Exhibit 1). records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 59 Government Bonds | Rate Expectations & Term Premiums The term premia and rate‑expectations tickers provide a model‑based decomposition of nominal government bond yields into two core components: (1) the expected path of future short‑term policy rates and (2) the residual term premium associated with holding longer‑dated securities. Derived from the Adrian-Crump-Moench (ACM) term-structure model, these measures quantify how much of the observed yield reflects investors’ policy expectations versus compensation for duration risk and uncertainty. Use cases Term premia tickers help separate yield movements driven by policy expectations from those reflecting changes in risk compensation. While the absolute values can be model‑dependent, the direction and co‑movement with yields often reveal the underlying narrative—whether markets are pricing policy shifts or reacting to changes in risk appetite and uncertainty. Calculation methodology We start with the spot rates generated from our Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Par/Spot Yields model which serves as the input zero-coupon yields for estimation. The ACM model is applied on these spot yields following a standard three-step procedure mentioned in the ACM paper. The yields are first demeaned and principal component analysis (PCA) is performed to extract the 5 most significant factors. Next, we run OLS regressions of one‑period excess returns on the factor vector to estimate return

Much as we had expected in our FOMC preview, the June SEP showed significant upward revisions to inflation for this year and small downward revisions to GDP growth and unemployment rate projections. FOMC participants raised the 2026 headline PCE inflation median projection 0.9pp, to 3.6% Q4/Q4 amid elevated oil prices, and boosted their core PCE inflation projection 0.6pp, to 3.3% Q4/Q4 (Figure 1). They also lifted the 2027 median inflation projections by 0.1pp for headline inflation, to 2.3% Q4/Q4, and by 0.3pp for core inflation, to 2.5% Q4/Q4. Interestingly, despite these large upgrades, the vast majority of participants (17 out of 18) saw inflation risks as tilted to the upside (Figure 3). Participants lowered the median GDP growth projections for this year by 0.2pp, to 2.2% Q4/Q4, given the weaker-than-expected GDP estimates for Q1, and they lowered their unemployment rate projection for 2026, by a tenth to 4.3%, bringing it in line with recent estimates. At the same time, most of the participants now see risks as balanced, while they saw them as skewed to the upside in March (Figure 2). Financial market participants, business leaders and households have no choice but to make decisions at all times based on their expectations, regardless of the information provided by central bankers. In the absence of any guidance by policymakers, the public is at risk of misunderstanding central bankers' intentions and of forming inaccurate beliefs, resulting in decisions and market pricing that might be costly to unwind for the economy as whole. In our view, a Fed that would cut back substantially on its communication would more likely find itself facing market pricing that it will deem inappropriate (eg, the market pricing a full rate hike at the time of a meeting when the FOMC would have no intention to raise rates). This would, in our view, ultimately complicate the FOMC's decision and is likely to result in more market volatility. As much academic research has found, forward guidance can also be a very powerful tool that can help ease or tighten financial conditions when needed, without needing policy rates to move much. Indeed, as former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke emphasized years ago, monetary policy operates largely through expectations, making communication and credibility central to its effectiveness. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 101 FX Hedge Cost For Developed Markets This measure tracks annualized FX hedge costs for major developed-market currency pairs across the 1M, 3M, 6M, and 1Y tenors. It uses Bloomberg spot and forward-point data to estimate the implied cost or benefit of hedging currency exposure over different horizons. The series provide a daily view of cross-currency carry and hedging pressure across EUR, USD, JPY, and GBP pairs. Use cases Investors use these series to compare the cost of hedging foreign-currency exposure across major funding and investment currencies. They assess whether hedge costs are becoming more or less punitive by tenor and identify where forward markets are pricing meaningful carry differentials. Portfolio managers can use them to evaluate the drag or pickup from hedging international bond, equity, or credit exposure, while strategists can monitor changes in hedge costs as a signal of monetary-policy divergence, funding stress, or cross-currency demand. Calculation methodology For each currency pair, we use their spot rates and the corresponding 1M, 3M, 6M, and 12M forward rates data. Hedge cost is calculated as forward points divided by spot, annualized using a 360-day convention based on the tenor length. For non-JPY-style quotations, the result is scaled by 0.01 to account for Bloomberg forward-point conventions. records.text: Virginia rejoins: Virginia exited the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) at the end of 2023. However, on 24 April, the state confirmed it would rejoin the scheme from 1 July and participate in the final two RGGI auctions of the year. This is significant, as Virginia’s emission profile is increasingly important within the scheme. The state is the second-largest emitting market in the programme following New York, based on Environmental Protection Agency data as of 2023. The AI infrastructure build-out should further accelerate power consumption and emissions growth, adding incremental allowance demand to an already tightening market. Renewable capacity remains limited in Virginia, with wind and solar accounting for only around 26% of total power generation at end-2025 (Figure 33). This leaves the state relatively more exposed to gas and other thermal generation as demand rises . RGA spot prices climbed to USD55.6 per short ton on 4 May following Virginia’s re- entry announcement, before settling at USD42.5t as at 17 June. The move reflects expectations of stronger future compliance demand and a tighter cap trajectory from 2027. The most important communication event is the monetary policy meeting, followed by the press release and press conference, eight times a year. Minutes are released four weeks later. But, they are an edited document, not a verbatim account. In March, June, September and December, the ECB releases fresh macro forecasts. Details matter, but it is crucial to watch end-point inflation forecasts paired with the implied market pricing of ECB policy rate trajectories. Economists vs market pricing of ECB trajectories To compare economists’ expectations for ECB trajectories, we use Bloomberg consensus expectations or the ECB’s own Survey of Monetary Analysts. For market pricing, we prefer the meeting-based OIS contracts. The ECB itself uses 3-month (3m) Euribor futures for its forecasts, with 3m Euribor fixing currently incorporating a 10- 15bp spread vs actual policy rates. Euribor futures are a liquid market, especially for the relevant longer-policy horizon. But with excess liquidity declining, the term funding element of Euribor pricing may gain in importance and consequently make it a less clean read-across for market policy expectations. Beyond rates: the ECB balance sheet matters too Of course, ECB policy is not limited to interest rates. The balance sheet is sizeable after big asset purchase programmes. records.text: 218/06/2026 Data centres update H2 2026: New hotspots, old constraints KEY MESSAGES Data-centre project pipelines are set to keep expanding globally, driven by AI competition and cost inflation, despite unchanged key constraints from grid and generation . The US will remain the largest data-centre market, we think, fuelled by strong pipelines in Texas and Virginia. Growth in Europe is likely to broaden beyond the ‘FLAP-D’ locations, with the Nordics and Spain gaining traction. Southeast Asia is emerging as a growth hub, but we expect rising power demand to test regional power systems . We think the market is overestimating copper demand for data centres. We believe copper data centre demand accounts for only 2% of global copper demand, and do not expect this share to grow. Battery storage for data centres will become increasingly crucial to smooth renewable generation, expedite grid connection queues and support on-site thermal generation – and in combination with solar, is vying to offer a potential alternative to gas for baseload power in the long-term. US supply-side constraints in grids and generation show limited signs of easing. We still see US power market tightness through to at least 2030,driving higher prices or slowing uncommitted data-centre growth. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 87 Corporate Bonds | Investment Grade and High-Yield Supply This measure captures daily U.S. corporate bond issuance activity across the Investment Grade (IG) and High Yield (HY) markets. The series track total issuance volume, duration- adjusted supply, weighted-average maturity, weighted-average coupon, and the number of bonds issued. Together, these metrics provide a standardized view of primary market financing activity and evolving issuance characteristics. Use cases Investors use these tickers to monitor corporate bond supply conditions, assess issuance trends, and evaluate the maturity and coupon profile of new debt coming to market. Applications include tracking primary market activity, measuring duration supply through 10-year equivalents, analyzing financing conditions and incorporating supply dynamics into portfolio construction and risk management frameworks. Calculation methodology Corporate bond issuance data are aggregated daily using bond-level issuance records. Notional amounts, maturities, and coupon rates are converted to numeric values prior to aggregation. Total notional (NOT) is calculated as the sum of issuance amounts. Ten-year equivalents (10Y) are calculated as issuance amount multiplied by original tenor divided by 10. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 61 Government Bonds | Swap Spread Carry & Roll Down Swap spread roll down and carry tickers quantify the expected return components arising from the relationship between swap rates and government bond yields under a stable curve assumption. Roll down captures how the swap spread evolves as both the swap and bond maturities shorten over time, while carry reflects the return earned from the differential between their respective forward and current spreads over a given horizon. Together, these measures provide a structured view of expected movements in swap spreads, isolating the effects of time and forward curve dynamics. They help investors assess relative value between swaps and government bonds, identify dislocations along the spread curve, and refine curve and spread trading strategies. Use cases These metrics have similar use cases as defined in the Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Carry & Roll Down Calculation methodology We first compute the Roll Down and Carry for the constant maturity bonds as well as the OIS rates using the methodology outlined in the Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Carry & Roll Down and Interest Rate Swaps | Carry & Roll Down, respectively. The swap spread roll down and carry are then defined as the difference between the corresponding swap and government bond values, providing a clear view of the relative curve and income dynamics between the two markets. The BoE, Riksbank and Norges Bank kept rates on hold with biases to hike. We now expect hikes from the BoE in November (from July previously), given weaker-than-expected inflation, the Riksbank in December (from September previously) and Norges Bank in September, with the risk of an earlier move on upside core inflation surprises. • The mid-cycle neutral bias echoes 1996-1997, when Chair Greenspan stayed cautious, not overreacting to strong macro data and trusting that heavy tech investment would lift productivity at a later stage. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 89 FX & EM Strategy Trade-Weighted Currency Indexes Trade-weighted currency indexes measure the value of a currency relative to the currencies of its major trading partners, with weights based on bilateral trade shares. Unlike simple bilateral exchange rates, they provide a broad gauge of external competitiveness. By adjusting for trade patterns, these indexes track a currency’s effective value against the global basket of partners. Use cases Investors use trade-weighted indexes to monitor competitiveness, inflation pass-through risk, and external balance adjustments. Central banks track them to evaluate real exchange rate misalignments. Portfolio managers employ them in cross-country comparisons, hedging strategies, and macroeconomic risk models. Strategists analyze index changes to anticipate policy responses and to assess currency impacts on trade, growth, and inflation. Calculation methodology We construct trade-weighted indexes by selecting a basket of partner currencies and applying bilateral trade weights derived from official trade flow data. Exchange rates are expressed in index form relative to a base year. We update weights periodically to reflect evolving trade shares. The index level is computed as the geometric average of bilateral rates adjusted by weights. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 11 Market-Implied | Pace of Central Bank Rate Moves This measure captures the market-implied pace of central bank adjustments. It identifies the market-implied policy change over a 12-month forward-looking period starting after the next market-implied 25bp change. By quantifying implied speed of rate moves, it provides a framework for analyzing the expected number of cuts or hikes by the central bank. Use cases Investors can use this measure to assess whether central banks are expected to act gradually or aggressively. It helps gauge potential volatility when markets price faster adjustments. Traders could incorporate it into risk models, particularly under stress scenarios that assume sharp policy moves. Calculation methodology We first identify the peak and trough of the curve using the methodology mentioned in the Market-Implied | Peak/Trough Central Bank Policy Rates. Next, the “months to next move” points are determined by Market-Implied | # of Months to Next Central Bank Move , marking the horizon to the upcoming hike or cut. The pace of central bank rate moves is then computed as the difference between the rate at the next move and the rate observed one year after that point. In cases where no rate hike or cut is priced within the 5-year horizon, or where the one- year-forward point after the next move lies beyond this horizon, a value of 60 is published. The loss of Qatari LNG supply driven by the Iran conflict was never sustainable for European gas markets owing to the need for gas storage to refill ahead of the winter, when natural gas demand is highest, especially given the strong rebound in Asia LNG demand since May. So, either LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz would start to normalize to allow European gas storage to refill, or TTF would have to rally to get it done by discouraging Asia LNG demand. The recently announced agreement between the US and Iran potentially allows for the former, leading us to keep our 2H26 TTF forecast largely unchanged at 41 EUR/MW, in line with current forwards. However, even with the imminent resumption of energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, we expect North West European natural gas storage levels, currently well below average, to only climb to 74% full ahead of this coming winter (Exhibit 1), the lowest level since 2013. It is complemented by the “months to peak” and “months to trough” tickers, which indicate the expected timing of these turning points. Use cases The peak/trough rates act as proxies for the terminal levels to which a central bank may hike or cut, providing a market-based benchmark for policy pricing. They help investors gauge the expected number and duration of hikes or cuts within the current regime. We complement the tickers with “months to next hike,” “months to next cut,” “pace of hikes,” “pace of cuts,” “months to peak,” and “months to trough.” These offer a more nuanced view of the policy cycle, and define the prevailing regime by signaling whether the curve reflects easing or tightening, and how long such conditions are likely to persist. Calculation methodology We construct the instantaneous (1-day) forward curve from OIS rates under no-arbitrage conditions across all tenors, using a combination of Cubic Spline and Linear Interpolation. After curve construction, we remove any outliers or spikes caused in the process to ensure a smooth, continuously differentiable curve. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 57 Government Bonds | 10-Year Equivalents | Sectors The sector-specific 10-Year Equivalent measure expresses interest rate risk within each maturity segment—such as bills, notes, or bonds—in terms of standardized 10-year government bond exposure. It represents the notional amount of 10-year bonds required to replicate the same rate risk as that particular sector. Use cases It shares similar use cases with Government Bonds | 10-Year Equivalents. These tickers express portfolio or sector-level interest rate sensitivity in standardized 10-year bond units, allowing investors to compare risk across maturities and sectors. By translating DV01 into an equivalent 10-year exposure, they provide a clearer and more intuitive view of rate risk concentration and portfolio positioning along the curve. Calculation methodology We compute the sector-specific 10-Year Equivalent by dividing each sector’s total DV01— calculated using the methodology described in Government Bonds | DV01 Risk—by the DV01 of the on-the-run 10-year government bond. Since DV01 measures the change in value for a one-basis-point move in yields, this ratio converts each sector’s interest rate risk into equivalent 10-year bond units. This allows for a standardized comparison of rate sensitivity across different maturity sectors within the portfolio. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 33 Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Forward Yields This section presents implied par forward yields derived from the constant maturity curve. Forward yields represent the coupon rate available today for a par bond issued at a future date with a specified maturity. Put differently, they translate the current spot curve into the par coupon that would apply over a future investment horizon. Use cases Strategists can use forward yields to analyze expectations for policy rates, curve steepening or flattening, and term premium changes. Portfolio and risk managers can use the historical depth of the of the output for backtesting the forward rate based signals and stress testing portfolio exposures to the parallel or twist shifts in the forward curve. Calculation methodology We first construct a discount curve from spot rates derived using the cubic spline methodology. Spot rates are converted into discount factors through an exponential transformation, ensuring a consistent mapping from the spot curve to present values. We then compute the par forward yield for each combination of forward-start horizon, n, and bond maturity, m. The par forward yield, f(n,m), is defined as the semi-annual coupon rate that prices a hypothetical bond to par, where the bond settles at future horizon n and matures at n+m. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 85 Interest Rate Swaptions | Implied Distribution Probabilities This measure captures the market-implied probability that interest rates will finish below specific thresholds at future horizons. It transforms option prices into outcome probability distributions. In a standardized way, the series quantify forward-looking risks by summarizing how option markets price the likelihood of different interest rate scenarios. Use cases Investors use these tickers to quantify probabilities of SOFR rates falling below, above, or between thresholds at specified horizons. They calculate above-threshold probabilities as one minus the ticker value, and ranges as the difference between tickers. Applications: scenario analysis, relative value trading, hedging design, and measuring the informational content of volatility surfaces beyond forwards and at-the-money implied vol. Calculation methodology We derive implied probabilities by fitting arbitrage-free SABR models to SOFR swaption vol surfaces, ensuring consistency with market quotes. We extract risk-neutral densities using numerical techniques that avoid negative probabilities. We then integrate these densities over specified thresholds, producing daily time series of terminal rate probabilities across maturities, horizons, and strike levels (see our primer). records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 47 Government Bonds | Weighted-Average Maturity Weighted-average maturity (WAM) summarizes the average time to repayment of outstanding government debt, weighted by par outstanding. It reflects how sovereigns manage refinancing risks by choosing longer or shorter maturities for issuance. By capturing the overall maturity profile of outstanding debt, it offers a clear view of refinancing timelines and the structure of sovereign borrowing. Use cases Investors use maturity profiles to evaluate refinancing risk and assess how sovereigns balance borrowing costs with rollover exposure. Economists can use it as a proxy for estimating the tenor of future issuances. when guidance to debt management is limited. Use WAM alongside DV01 to assess refinancing risk. WAM describes the term structure and DV01 quantifies interest-rate sensitivity. Together, these measures provide a much more complete view of rollover exposure. Calculation methodology We calculate a portfolio's weighted-average maturity by multiplying each bonds's time to maturity by its weight in the portfolio. The weighting is done based on the par amount held in the portfolio. We then sum the weighted maturity to produce the weighted- average maturity of sovereign portfolio. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 23 Commodity Trading Advisor (CTA) | Positions This indicator estimates model-implied CTA positions across major asset classes, derived from systematic trend-following signals. CTAs typically establish long or short exposures based on momentum, and this measure summarizes their positioning. It provides transparency into systematic investor behavior and serves as a proxy for one of the most influential quantitative trading strategies in global financial markets. Use cases Investors track CTA positioning to assess potential sources of momentum-driven market moves. By monitoring aggregate exposures, they can identify situations where systematic funds may amplify price trends or contribute to reversals. Portfolio managers incorporate this measure into risk models, while strategists use it to anticipate flow-driven effects across equities, bonds, and commodities. Calculation methodology We estimate CTA positions using the Morgan Stanley Cross-Asset Trend-Following framework. Trend signals derive from exponentially weighted moving average crossovers transformed into standardized scores. We weight signals by volatility-targeted risk budgets across asset classes. Aggregating positions under assumed US$250–400 billion AUM yields notional estimates, which exhibit correlations above 0.85 with benchmark CTA indices (see Understanding CTA Positioning And Forecasting CTA Flows). records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 7 Global Risk Demand Index The Global Risk Demand Index (GRDI) measures aggregate investor appetite for risk by comparing the relative performance of risky versus safe assets across major markets. It condenses signals from multiple asset classes into a single daily indicator, with a standardized version (STGRDI) expressed as a z-score to allow for historical comparability and mean-reversion analysis. Use cases Investors use the GRDI to monitor global shifts in risk sentiment and to identify turning points in volatility or risk-on/risk-off dynamics. Strategists apply it as an overlay to FX, credit, and equity views, while portfolio managers use it to calibrate exposure to cyclical versus defensive assets. Extreme standardized values serve as contrarian trading signals. Calculation methodology We construct ten sub-indices (GRDI1–GRDI10), each comparing a risky asset index with a safer benchmark (e.g., EM vs. DM bonds, base vs. precious metals, high-yield vs. investment-grade credit). Each sub-index is rebased to 100 and updated daily using relative price changes. We compute GRDIIDX as the equally weighted geometric mean of all sub-indices, then standardize with a three-month rolling z-score to obtain STGRDI (see Global Risk Demand Index and its US patent). records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 7 EIA Weekly Summary The total crude inventory draw in the US was 17.2 mln bbls WoW, taking total US crude inventories to their lowest level since March 1985. US commercial crude stocks drew by 8.3 mln bbls last week, a sizeable draw. The US SPR continued to draw as part of the IEA coordinated SPR release. SPR inventories fell 8.9 mln bbls WoW, implying a weekly withdrawal rate of ~1.3 mbpd. Stocks at Cushing drew by 1.6 mln bbls WoW to 20.0 mln bbls, a level often viewed as the operational floor for Cushing. Crude production was broadly flat WoW at 13.8 mbpd. US crude exports fell by 0.5 mbpd WoW, to 4.3 mbpd. This was flat on US crude exports for this week last year. US crude imports also fell WoW by 0.8 mbpd, pushing imports below the 5Y seasonal range again. Despite crude exports slowing, a corresponding decline in crude imports is keeping net imports into the US low and helping drive crude inventory draws. US refinery runs rose by 230 kbpd WoW, pushing runs above the 5Y seasonal range. The uptick in runs was driven by a 114 kbpd rise in PADD 2 runs, as refiners in the region raised utilisation levels by 2.9pp WoW to over 100% utilisation. Overall, US refinery utilisation rates rose by 1.4pp WoW to 96.7%, with refinery runs sitting 1.5% above average seasonal levels. This marks a 10-month high in US refinery runs. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 18 June 2026 11 borrow reserves to meet their needs: initially in repo and unsecured markets and then via the ECB. It would be a point when non-linearities can emerge in money market rates. Reserve requirements: unknown new floor Euro Area banks have a minimum reserve requirement of 1% of specific liabilities. Historically, when reserve levels reached close to this min requirement, demand for reserves increased and money market rates priced higher. However, after the full phase- in of liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) requirements in 2018, it is now likely that banks will want to hold greater levels of reserves than seen pre-2018. In the last two years, Euro Area banks have held LCR ratios broadly stable at 155-160% by replacing reserves with other high-quality liquid assets (HQLA). As ECB’s QT continues reducing reserve levels, the moment banks start borrowing from the ECB via regular operations could be determined by how low banks are willing to take their reserves as a percentage of total HQLA – see the report, Prepare for non-linearities, Jan. 2026. Impact on money market rates and OMO usage As demand for reserves begins to increase, banks can increase borrowing in money markets to increase their level of holdings. All else equal, this would increase money market rates, such as Repo, Euribor and €STR (all relative to ECB rates). What stood out from today's decision? First, the MPC may, on paper, be more divided than in April – but there is a stronger consensus to keep Bank Rate on hold for now. Two members (Pill and Greene) opted for a rate hike, as we expected. But we think there is a growing consensus for a long hold given the more favourable economic and geopolitical backdrop. Second, for the MPC, recent data outturns combined with an Iran/US deal have meant that the risk around second-round effects has receded. Indeed, while the MPC still sees upside risks to inflation, lower wage and price inflation has given the MPC more confidence that price pressures may be more contained for now. Put simply, despite an inevitable inflation wave in the coming months, the MPC may be willing to tolerate and look through a temporary bump in price momentum. Third, the MPC has retained full optionality heading into summer. Despite better data and a dramatic fall in energy prices over the last week, the MPC avoided sounding too dovish. The outperformance of A-shares was driven by indices with higher AI hardware exposure, such as ChiNext (+22% yoy) and STAR (+198% yoy). Conversely, the offshore index continues to be weighed down by quick commerce subsidies and rising AI Capex. Sector divergence: SOE profit growth picked up to +7% yoy in 1Q26 (vs. +1% in n 2025), while POE growth slowed down to +4% yoy in 1Q26 (from +11% in 2025). At the sector level, upstream and technology sectors maintained robust momentum, led by Materials (+73% yoy), Tech Hardware (+25%), and Energy (+48%). In contrast, growth in consumer and property-related sectors remained subdued, with Retailing (-50%) and Autos (-27%) both contracting sharply. Looking ahead: We have recently revised down our MSCI China EPS growth n forecasts to 8%/12% for 2026/27E, while maintaining our CSI300 EPS growth forecasts at 20%/12%, supported by the ongoing “Soft vs. Hard” tech divide. Consensus estimates for ChiNext and STAR50 also point to robust growth of +34%/+25% and +83%/+60% yoy for 2026/27E, respectively. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 17 Market-Implied | Quarterly Policy Rate Path This measure tracks market-implied central bank policy rates for major developed-market economies. The series convert overnight-index forward curves into expected policy-rate levels at future quarter-end and year-end dates, providing a standardized view of how markets price the path of policy rates across currencies. Use cases Strategists use this series to (1) compare expected policy paths across economies, (2) monitor repricing around central-bank meetings and macro data, (3) assess cross-market relative value, and (4) train quantitative models. Risk managers running scenario stress tests with quarterly projections use it to compare policy scenarios with market-implied policy rates. Calculation methodology We construct the instantaneous (1-day) forward curve from OIS rates using the methodology outlined in the Market-Implied | Peak/Trough Central Bank Policy Rates. The curve is then cleaned to remove large discontinuities, interpolated using a cubic spline, and sampled at future policy-rate reference dates. Year-end tickers capture the curve-implied rate at each future December 31 date, while quarter-end tickers capture the next nine quarter-end points. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 45 Government Bonds | Weighted-Average Yield | Sectors Weighted-average yield by sector summarizes the yield profile across key segments of the government bond market, such as bills, notes, and bonds. It highlights sector-level differences in funding costs and investor compensation across maturity segments. By breaking the curve into distinct buckets, it provides a more granular view of pricing trends and relative valuation across the sovereign debt spectrum. Use cases It shares similar use cases with Government Bonds | Weighted Average Yield. These tickers offer a more detailed view of yield dynamics across different maturity segments, helping investors analyze curve behavior and identify relative value opportunities within specific tenor buckets. Calculation methodology We compute sector specific weighted average yield of a portfolio by partitioning the bonds into a time to maturity defined sectors. Within each partition we compute the weighted average yield by multiplying each bonds's yield-to-maturity by its weight in that sector. The weighting is done based on the par amount held in that sector of portfolio.We then sum the weighted yields to produce the weighted average yield of portfolio sector. records.text: ergy and food) that are deemed sensitive to slack. For detail, see Box 2 in "Measures of underlying inflation for the euro area ", ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 4/2018. Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) is one of the measures of underlying inflation monitored by the ECB. PCCI aims to capture common developments across different items in the consumption basket representing the more persistent part of inflation. PCCI is constructed using a generalised dynamic factor model, where a common factor is estimated across 12 eurozone countries and around 1000 monthly price series. The PCCI is then calculated as the weighted average of the estimated common components. Using this approach the PCCI should exclude short-term volatility due to temporary/transient factors and reflect medium- and long-run movements in inflation. See detail, Bańbura and Bobeica: PCCI – a data-rich measure of underlying inflation in the euro area , ECB Statistics Paper Series, October 2020.

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 29 Headline CPI Inflation Surprises Morgan Stanley Inflation Surprise tickers provide individual country inflation surprise indices for 7 DM and 10 EM regions, as well as normalized surprise indices for DM and EM aggregates. Positive surprises occur when reported inflation exceeds expectations, while negative surprises arise when outcomes fall short. It quantifies the gap between anticipated and realized inflation, offering a standardized metric for economic data shocks. Use cases The 1M/1Q tickers track daily headline CPI surprises versus Bloomberg medians without waiting for month or quarter labels. The 6M/1Y indices gauge whether inflation surprises are accumulating, distinguishing one-offs from sustained trends. Countries can be compared consistently, while equally weighted DM/EM aggregates serve as broad barometers of global inflation pressure, preventing large economies from dominating the signal. Calculation methodology We calculate 1M/1Q inflation surprise indices by subtracting the Bloomberg median survey estimate from realized headline inflation (monthly for all regions except New Zealand). The 6M/1Y balance indices sum the previous 6/12 (2/4) most recent monthly (quarterly) surprises, reflecting the cumulative buildup of inflation surprises. Aggregate DM and EM versions of these series serve as broad measures of global inflation pressure. To build the 1M aggregates, we normalize each region’s monthly (quarterly) surprises

AI’s increased use as a geopolitical lever could widen US-RoW divergences to the USD’s benefit in H2. AI is increasingly being viewed by governments as a strategic dependency rather than a purely commercial technology, with the latest US export-control episode around Anthropic’s top models adding to this concern (see here). These latest US export restrictions suggest the AI control perimeter is widening from chips and data-center inputs to also include models, cloud access, employees, and end users. (17 Apr 2026) Middle East conflict de-escalation is positive for gold: Gold has not played its traditional safe haven role during the conflict, with supply shocks harder to hedge than demand shocks. The conflict has created 2 headwinds for gold: 1) higher bond yields; 2) pressure on fiscal balances of oil and gas importers, driving some gold sales (e.g. Turkey). Against this backdrop, de-escalation should be supportive. Our oil strategist sees lower oil prices than previously expected, which should ease pressure on central banks either to sell gold or to tighten monetary policy. In the latest WGC central bank survey, a record 45% of respondents expect their gold reserves to increase over the next 12m. China’s PBOC has already accelerated purchases, buying 23t between March and May, versus 19t in the previous 12m. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 81 Inflation Swaps | Core CPI fixings The CPI fixings market is one in which investors can take a view on each month's CPI release. Each month's NSA CPI index which is a price index level is actively traded in the market. We get a monthly headline CPI print after seasonally adjusting it. After removing our forecasts for food and energy for the month, we can calculate core CPI fixing for the upcoming month inflation print. Use cases Food and energy components can be volatile and hence can be stripped to get the underlying trend in inflation. These tickers will be helpful in understanding how market pricing of monthly inflation prints has evolved over time. The ticker value stabilizes after end of the month. Calculation methodology We get a good estimate for energy commodities towards the end of the month from retail gas station prices. Throughout the month we use gasoline futures. For energy services we use time series modelling using natural gas futures and for electricity we use EIA estimates. For estimating food inflation, we consider food futures. records.text: ab 18 June 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Eurozone: Inflation likely to fall in June Some broadening of inflation, but not too concerning yet May HICP breakdown showed some inflation broadening, but not too concerning yet. We forecast headline inflation to fall 0.3pp to 2.9% in June and expect that the ECB will pause at the July meeting, but then hike rates by another 25bps to 2.5% in September. Underlying inflation measures on balance up in May The final Eurozone HICP estimate for May (published on 17 June) confirmed a 0.2pp increase to 3.2% y/y, while core inflation was revised slightly higher (+0.1pp), rising by 0.4pp to 2.6%. We calculate that around three quarters of the increase in core was driven by volatile and seasonal services - namely transportation (airfares), package holidays, and accommodation - which typically fluctuate between March and June due to Easter timing. It’s a welcome step toward de-escalation, but we stress that the situation remains volatile. The reported deal sounds like a 60‑day ceasefire extension aimed at reopening the Strait, lifting the US blockade, and creating negotiating space, without resolving core disputes (nuclear program, missiles, proxies). Market relevance hinges on the details, especially sanctions relief/asset unfreezing, enrichment limits, and uranium stockpiles. In the near-term, both sides claiming “victory” raises the bar for restarting the conflict, but implementation risks, miscalculation, and potential re- escalations remain key tail risks. With a tentative, lasting peace framework in place, the first LNG tanker (Disha) transited out of the Strait of Hormuz with transponders on, and is enroute to Dahej, India, having loaded at Ras Laffan June 12–13. Only about eight LNG vessels remain inside the Strait (two with transponders off), but Middle East LNG flows are still constrained; even if the Strait fully reopens soon, exports are expected to take 2-3 months to normalize. This relative value expression allows investors to exploit a substantial insurance premium against rate hikes, removes outright duration beta, while not requiring a near-term dovish pivot by the Fed. The main risk is if fiscal stimulus arrives before the mid-term elections, which would justify currently elevated levels of near-term inflation expectations. 10s20s SONIA Steepener We think front-end rates embed a meaningful risk premium, leaving room for tightening expectations to decline. Federal Reserve Commentary June FOMC: We’ve got a task force for that The FOMC held rates and issued a short statement that reaffirms the focus on price stability and ample reserves. The new dot plot shows 9 of 18 participants favoring rate hikes this year, as they raised their inflation projections. We are changing our Fed call to a hold through end-2027. • The FOMC maintained the fed funds rate target range unchanged at 3.50-3.75%, as widely anticipated. • The new FOMC statement was shortened considerably, removing any forward guidance, the easing bias that had caused three hawkish members to dissent at the April meeting, and the committee's risk assessment. The statement was adopted by unanimous vote. • The statement emphasized the committee's determination to bring inflation back to the 2% target, affirming that the "Committee will deliver price stability, " without mentioning the maximum employment side of the mandate. This raises, in our view, questions about a possible change in the FOMC

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 97 EMFX Idiosyncratic Risk Premiums This measure isolates the idiosyncratic component of EM currency risk premia by stripping out the influence of common global drivers such as the US dollar, global rates, and broad risk sentiment. The resulting series captures the portion of FX returns that is specific to each country, providing a standardized measure of currency-specific risk that is comparable across EM economies. The tickers are expressed in standardized units, allowing users to assess whether a currency is trading rich or cheap relative to its own history after controlling for global macro factors. Use cases Investors use these series to distinguish between global and local drivers of EMFX performance. This is particularly useful when assessing whether currency moves reflect shifts in US rates and dollar dynamics or changes in domestic fundamentals such as policy credibility, external balances, or political risk. The measures can be used to identify relative value opportunities across EM currencies, construct cross-sectional trades that neutralize global beta, and monitor episodes of country-specific stress or improvement. Strategists also use them to evaluate the effectiveness of macro narratives, test whether markets are overpricing local risks, and track the evolution of idiosyncratic premia through policy cycles and external shocks. records.text: for the Fed to shrink reserve levels over time. Sequencing will matter: the more likely path is to first reduce structural demand, and then adjust the size of the balance sheet accordingly. On the balance sheet, a natural area for evolution is the weighted average maturity (WAM) of the portfolio. The Fed is already moving in this direction – replacing runoff MBS with Treasury bills and directing incremental balance sheet growth toward bills. Over the longer run, the Fed has yet to finalize its desired long-run composition of its Treasury portfolio, with the choice broadly between matching the maturity profile of outstanding universe or maintaining a shorter- duration portfolio aligned with its short-term liabilities. A shift toward a shorter WAM appears the more likely outcome and already appears to have support among some on the committee, such as Governor Waller. In sum, the changes most likely to garner broad support are a shortening of portfolio WAM and a reduction in reserve demand via adjustments to liquidity regulations. Both of these would satisfy the philosophical aim of running a leaner balance sheet. 18 June 2026 9 Barclays | Federal Reserve Commentary

records.text: t. Per the LFS, self-employment rose by ~170k in the past three months, while employment fell by 70k. For the first time in a long time, it seems like the LFS and HMRC data might be aligned - payrolls don't account for self-employment. We are in two minds on how much weight to put on the LFS numbers. Is it really possible this surge in self-employment is real when demand for workers generally seems lacklustre? Could it be just a delayed ONS normalisation of the employment/self- employment split, given self-employment is still running 10% down on 2019 levels? On the other hand, given strength in some white-collar services sectors such as ICT, where self-employment does seem plausible, perhaps this data is worth taking at face value? All in all, the jobless rate, we think, is ~5%, and as such an ongoing evidence of ample labour market slack. We continue to see the jobless rate ticking up this year, albeit remaining sub-5.5%. We have long argued that such a shift is less likely, including variations on this where reserves are run up the demand curve, and marginal reserves are created actively via the ceiling tools (SRF and discount window). That is because, the risks are asymmetric and reserve demand is not static. The Fed has experience first hand that under scarcity-like conditions, relatively small declines in reserves (or increases in non-reserve liabilities outside the Fed’s control) can generate disproportionately large and nonlinear moves in short-term rates. Such a regime could only work if it relies on the Fed’s ceiling tools, but that would require a complete elimination of stigma Governor Bowman has suggested a preference for reserves closer to scarce than ample. Even so, underlying reserve demand appears elevated, limiting the scope for a meaningful reduction from current levels. That means there is limited benefit to such a system, as it does not achieve much of a reduction in reserves, while the downside risk of funding market blow up like in 2019 is real. This implies that any durable reduction in reserves would likely need to come through lower structural demand. Adjustments to liquidity regulations that reduce banks’ demand for reserves would create space for the Fed to shrink reserve levels over time. Candidates and political parties have advanced few policy proposals so far, n making it difficult to assess the potential implications for France’s economic and fiscal outlook. But recent communication suggests that all candidates (except Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left) would support a further reduction in the deficit, with varying views on the accompanying policy mix. France’s pay-as-you-go pension system is likely to remain a highly contentious issue, with many candidates trying to de-emphasise a change to the retirement age and voicing openness to a move towards a partially funded model. Rassemblement National dropped its pledge to leave the European Union and n the Euro almost ten years ago. But the party’s leadership could still adopt a more confrontational stance with Brussels, for example on the topic of France’s contribution to the European Union’s budget, migration, and energy markets. The centrist parties remain strongly pro-European, with Philippe, Gabriel Attal in the centre, and Raphaël Glucksmann on the centre-left all unequivocally calling for further European integration. Market pricing of oil today is certainly below the ECB’s baseline from June (Exhibit 2), and that creates downside to its inflation forecasts. But it’s still above the ECB’s mild scenario in June and not far from the its baseline in March. For gas the picture is similar, with prices close to the March baseline (Exhibit 3). With that in mind, and given the usual ECB bias, we are not saying a hold in September is unthinkable. In fact, unlike last week after the ceasefire news, a “one and done” is probably now more likely than a third hike. But we would argue that a hold in September would need even lower energy prices or levels not far from where we are today coupled with dovish surprises in the data. Data may not help, here. Short-term, the drop in energy prices may actually bring about a sentiment data recovery. Core inflation may be a key factor for the ECB, too. Remember that the persistence of ex-energy inflation was a key argument against cuts a few months ago, and since March, the ECB has been very vocal about concerns that indirect and second-round effects of energy prices could be faster and larger this time round. Europe price competitiveness vis a vis China have deteriorated significantly since Covid and it has not yet recovered. China’s ‘anti-involution’ policies, which aim to counter excess capacity, and the Chinese yuan’s recent rise against the euro, have increased the price of China manufacturing goods. The gap remain large, with European producer prices still 35% higher than 2020. • As the RHS chart shows, there is a strong correlation between the relative producer prices between EU and China and the widening of the trade deficit with China. None of these flows alone are indigestible for the market, or enough to run an outright bearish view. But we do see them collectively as a headwind and source of volatility. This period of flow-driven volatility will then turn to more fundamental drivers mid-July, with Q2 earnings. We like being long SPX optionality for delta replacement or hedging. For downside, we continue to look at July 10th expiry tail hedge, capturing the liquidity events but expiring ahead of earnings. Indicatively, SPY US 10Jul26 720/700 Put Spread, 1.77 (0.46%) Offer, -10d, 10.3 x Max PnL, vs 745.6. Earnings upside: One lesson from price action YTD is to follow the earnings revisions. Change to our FOMC rate call In light of the FOMC's hawkish turn, which appears squarely focused on restoring price stability, and given the participants' upward revisions in the dots for both 2026 and 2027, we now expect the FOMC to maintain rates unchanged until the end of 2027. We were previously expecting the FOMC to keep rates unchanged this year but to cut them 25bp in March 2027, shortly after the committee would see inflation moderating in early 2027. However, the latest dot plot indicates that a growing set of policymakers is willing to address the persistently elevated inflation with higher rates. As noted above, the dot plot is consistent with our expectation of no rate change, although the distribution of dots suggests that it would take little for a majority of the participants to favor a rate hike this year. records.text: M Idea 4 Rates Strategy: High Bar For Near-term Hikes Fabio Bassanin The market reaction was relatively muted, although front-end MPC pricing repriced lower. The BoE reiterated its focus on the risk of second-round effects; however, according to the minutes, these pressures appear modest and may take time to materialize. As such, in our view, the bar for near-term rate hikes remains high. That said, the BoE retains a tightening bias, and the market continues to price slightly more than one hike over the remainder of the year and around 40bp of cumulative tightening through April (see Exhibit 2 ). In this context, we would highlight that receiving the September MPC meeting, which is priced at around ~13bp of cumulative hikes at the time of writing, looks relatively attractive. The likelihood of near-term hikes appears limited, while front-end MPCs should remains relatively insulated from both domestic and global market drivers, as well as any potential rebound in energy prices. That said, front-end rates remain somewhat elevated when considering the recent decline in inflation expectations. In Exhibit 3 , we plot average RPI fixing fixings %Y against the M7 SONIA contract. The two series have displayed a high degree of correlation in recent months; however, the M7 future appears to have lagged the recent repricing lower in inflation expectations. Pay growth: Private sector regular pay growth came in at 2.94%3M/Y, in line with our forecast, with the March monthly print revised up a touch. The monthly reading was robust in April (0.55%M), as is normally the case given this is the month when most UK pay settlements are revised, and when the National Living Wage starts to bind. We are a bit surprised by stronger white-collar sector pay growth in April, vs. trade & hospitality. But overall, ex-bonus pay growth in the lower-paid sectors (3.5%3M/Y) is still ~1pp higher than in finance & business services (2.5%3M/Y). All in all private sector pay growth looks target consistent, aided this year by a "normalised" hike in the NLW (4.1% on top of a cumulative 48.7% increase between April 2019 and April 2025). records.text: European Rates Weekly 18 June 2026 Citi Research 2 ECB speakers have all agreed this week that the inflation shock will not be reabsorbed quickly, inferring that the hike premium is likely to stick even amid lower oil prices. While (right) tail risk has arguably decreased, duration is unlikely to sustain a bullish regime, and we rather favour positioning for lower vol by receiving € 2s5s30s. The damage has been done already, ECB speakers agree. T op-left € vols closed broadly unchanged on Thursday despite Wednesday’s hawkish FOMC, with 9 out of 18 officials seeing higher rates at the end of the year. On this side of the Atlantic, such shift followed several ECB speakers (including Nagel, Lane, Makhlouf) agreeing that price pressures are lingering despite the emergence of a US-Iran deal. This corroborates our view that even as oil prices retreat, a further removal of hike premium seems unlikely from here. Front-end tail risk being faded. Nonetheless, the priced balance of risk around € front-end has extended its normalization, with both right-and left-tail risks cheapening towards early March levels (Figure 1). Market pricing is such that fading 3m payer skew (Figure 2) on 1s still gives a substantially higher buffer than selling receiver’s (Figure 3). Historically, selling skew via costless 1x2 structures has resulted in losses, higher for right- than for left-tail. We are of the view that the evolution of the economy between now and year-end will result in a slight easing of the tightening stance then, and we see, on balance, a rate cut in July 2027. The biggest risk to our view pertains to regulatory decisions (i.e. the NLW hike) and the easing of the fiscal drag. All in all, we see a prolonged hold ahead - as has been our view since the March meeting. Rates strategy: The market reaction was relatively muted, although front-end MPC pricing repriced lower. While the BoE reiterated its focus on the risk of second- round effects and retains a tightening bias, the bar for near-term rate hikes remains high. Despite this, markets continue to price around 30bp of cumulative tightening by year-end, leaving front-end MPC pricing looking somewhat cheap, in our view. That said, we remain mindful of domestic uncertainty in the near term and continue to favour curve steepeners, with 10s20s SONIA steepeners remaining our preferred expression. No single issue better encapsulates France’s fiscal and demographic challenges than its pension system.5 The Pension Advisory Council now forecasts that the system balance will continue to deteriorate after 2030 if no further measures are taken (Exhibit 12). 5 The pay-as-you-go nature of the system has meant that, with population aging and labour productivity slowing, the retirement age has had to increase to keep pension benefits stable and the system in balance. Regional divergence remains considerable and for now we do not see conditions for a reversal; we remain OW LatAm and EMEA EM versus UW EM Asia within the broader OW allocation. Since late 2022, when risk premia and yields peaked in EMEA EM post the Russia-Ukraine energy shock, EMEA EM and LatAm have considerably out- performed EM Asia. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures. 21/06/2026 2 A final whistle will not reset the score: Oil prices coming off should, all else equal, benefit Asia FX. However, as we outlined in FX: Comparing flow dynamics for the JPY, KRW and TWD on 15 June, we expect flow dynamics to remain bearish and overshadow the impact of lower oil prices. Foreign investor flows skew most bearish for the KRW, while domestic institutional and retail flows skew more bearish for the JPY and TWD. The JPY remains our preferred funder in North Asia, with fundamentals and flows weighing on the currency. What’s more, and for a number of reasons, we do not think an end to the conflict means US Treasury yields would return to their pre-war levels. First, the market’s link to oil prices had already weakened, and yields are already higher than oil prices would suggest by 15 – 20bp, reflecting economic strength. Second, inflation risks have broadened recently and we think a mere cooling of headline inflation will be insufficient for markets to un-price inflation concerns. Third, an end to the conflict may ultimately end up bringing more attention to long-term issues such as fiscal deficits , and investors may come to a realisation that the evolving Treasury buyer base is more price sensitive. Finally, an end to the conflict could add to economic strength as consumer sentiment improves, alongside the possi bility of more wealth effects forming a rally in risk assets

records.text: Following the profit growth: refreshing GS China Growth Portfolio To help investors identify high-conviction growth opportunities with compelling n risk/reward profiles, we have refreshed our GS China Growth Portfolio, selecting 25 premier names across the China A-share and H-share markets. Our selection process systematically leverages corporate disclosures, earnings call transcripts, profit guidance, and NDR notes to target companies aligned with our core structural themes. To ensure the portfolio remains highly selective and geared toward high-performing n leaders, we have upgraded our screening framework across three key dimensions: a) Near-term catalysts: we prioritize companies with clear operational o tailwinds, specifically focusing on price increases, Capex expansion, or overseas market penetration. Eligible constituents must have explicitly discussed these strategic drivers in their recent earnings calls or corporate announcements; b) Robust growth profile: we have raised our growth threshold, now requiring o an estimated 2025–27E EPS CAGR of greater than 10%, compared to >5% EPS CAGR previously; c) Positive earnings momentum: selected companies must demonstrate o positive revision trends, defined as an average upward revision of at least 1% in their 2026/2027E EPS estimates over the trailing month. The refreshed portfolio exhibits a highly robust fundamental profile, with the 25 n constituents having a median market cap/ADVT/25-27E EPS CAGR of US$16bn/US$249mn/39%.

records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research The war in Iran has diverted attention away from one of Europe’s key macroeconomic challenges: weak competitiveness. We highlighted this theme in our European 2026 outlook, and the focus on competitiveness vis- à-vis China, in particular, is growing. China is the EU’s second largest trading partner for goods, and the goods deficit with China is widening again and is close to the pandemic record level. The health of the EU-China trade relationship in general matters a lot for Europe’s macro prospects. After China joined the WTO, the global economy experienced its first “China shock”. Chinese exports surged worldwide and advanced economies’ export shares declined. Europe is now facing “China Shock 2.0” as China’s export share rises again. There are two key channels through which this shock can transmit to Europe. One channel is the potential for imported deflation. We discussed this in a recent note. This risk needs continuous monitoring, but the conclusion was the risks were overstated at this point. The other channel is the competitive threat to European exports. Competitiveness is the focus of this chartbook. Now seems the perfect time to share some insights. Second, headlines from “ECB sources” often follow right after policy meetings and are usually a tool for Governing Council members to flag divergence of views across decision makers. What are the monetary policy instruments? Interest rate policy is the ECB’s main tool at the moment. The central bank sets three policy rates: the deposit rate, currently at 2.25% (and most relevant given excess liquidity), the main refinancing rate (2.40%) and the marginal lending rate (2.65%). A conventional rate hike/cut is equivalent to 25bp. The “unconventional” toolbox has grown a lot over the past few years, especially during long periods when policy rates were at the effective lower bound” (ELB) and/or when the transmission mechanism was judged to be impaired. This can show in the passthrough of policy rate changes to market rates, bank lending conditions and volumes, the real economy or uneven transmission to individual Euro area members. These tools include long-term liquidity operations (LTROs), asset purchases (Asset Purchase Programme – i.e., more conventional QE, or PEPP, the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme) or purchase programmes that have not been activated, such as the OMT (Outright Monetary Transactions) or the TPI (Transmission Protection Instrument). On the monetary policy side, we believe the period between early 1996 and the end of 1997 offers a good template for the Fed's outlook today. Back then, large investments in information technology equipment and software were a big driver of the macro and market outlook, while inflation had begun to moderate but was still above target. After aggressive tightening in the early 90s, the Fed took policy rates to 6% before resuming modest easing in 1995 and early 1996, with policy rates ending at 5.25%. The recent reduction in fuel prices announced by the Ministry of Finance also adds a downward bias to our June and July forecasts. Hence, we now lower our 2026 year-end inflation forecast to 4.0% (from 4.2% previously), still above the 3% target of Chile’s central bank (BCCh). However, we expect a convergence towards the target over the following year, as supply shocks dissipate, demand remains soft and a stronger CLP curbs imported-goods inflation. Our projection for 2027 year-end inflation is 3.1%. El Niño threat: The likelihood of a strong El Niño episode has been increasing. During a strong El Niño, Chile typically experiences higher rainfall in the central and southern regions. Overall, while Chile is less exposed than some regional peers, El Niño episodes still introduce additional volatility to the inflation outlook and near-term growth path, mainly due to the following reasons: ▪ Damage to crop production, both locally and globally, adds to inflation pressures in food prices, at a gradual pace. For the 14.9 GW of global data-centre capacity added in 2025, this amounts to total copper demand of 402–536 kt, averaging 31.5 kt per 1GW. China’s AI data-centre copper demand is at the lower end of our estimate, closer to 27t/MW. This reflects the siting of facilities in industrial parks, allowing the use of existing grid architecture and thus eliminating the need for extensive distribution and connectivity works. While Chinese legacy semiconductor chips require more hardware support, the modest capacity per site and use of pre-built energy infrastructure offsets the need for greater copper intensity, in our view. The US campus-style facilities, meanwhile, require extensive on-site distribution, pushing intensity toward the higher end of the range at 35–36t/MW. Data centres are a marginal part of the copper picture: In 2025, data centre demand accounted for 2% of global copper demand. We estimate that share will remain about the same in 2026. In the US, new projects are becoming increasingly constrained by grid availability and long grid interconnection queues (see page 11). Indeed, we see grid constraints as a headwind for data centre growth and as a result, copper demand, both of which could also be dampened by emerging signs of popular resistance to data centres in the US. Now that Burnham has convincingly won that by-election, and looks set to challenge PM Kier Starmer, we think questions will be raised about the impact of potential changes to the policy mix. We still see a fiscally responsible shift to the left as the most likely outcome, but acknowledge markets will need some reassurance over Burnham’s commitment to the fiscal rules - for more see UK politics: A slow Burnham (Part 2) dated 19 June. Elsewhere, budget season will kicks off in Europe, in September. But term premia across Europe are back to their lows and we think fail to reflect potential for fiscal and headline risks, with political risks building into 2027 as key elections approach. Still a lot of supply to digest. June and May were amongst the heaviest supply months in 2026 across G4, our net supply estimates showed (Figure 2). While this was led by the UK and the US, German supply will only keep rising from here (Figure 3). What’s more, we see potential for a 30y German syndication in the next two weeks. The current amount outstanding on the 2056 (30y) has already reached EUR28.5bn, which we see as an indication that a new 30y is likely (the last 30y, the 2054s, currently has an amount outstanding of EUR29bn). Moreover, it has been a while since a new 30y has been launched (over 400 days). Issuing in H1 rather than in H2 (Sep) may be more strategic ahead of the Jan 2027 Dutch PF transition

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 55 Government Bonds | 10-Year Equivalents The 10-Year Equivalent measure expresses a portfolio’s interest rate risk in terms of standardized 10-year government bond exposure. This metric represents the notional amount of 10-year bonds required to replicate the same interest rate risk as the portfolio. Use cases The 10-Year Equivalent translates interest-rate sensitivity into standardized 10-year bond units, enabling like-for-like comparison of risk across maturities, sectors, and currencies. It shares similar use cases with Government Bonds | DV01 Risk. Portfolio managers use it to size positions and design hedges—often with 10-year futures or swaps—to target, neutralize, or rebalance DV01 efficiently. Calculation methodology We compute the 10-Year Equivalent by dividing the portfolio's total DV01 computed using the methodology mentioned in the Government Bonds | DV01 Risk by the on the run 10Y bond. Since DV01 represents the change in value for a one-basis-point move in yields, this ratio effectively scales the portfolio’s risk into 10-year bond units. It is expressed in local currency terms per one million notional. In simple terms, if the resulting value is 100 it implies that the portfolio carries the same rate risk as holding a $100 million notional 10Y note.
