To compute roll down for a given constant maturity tenor, we take the difference between the current par yields of the two maturities corresponding to the desired horizon. Carry reflects the expected return from holding a bond over a specified period, incorporating both coupon income and the opportunity cost of financing through the repo rate. For a constant maturity point, we assume a hypothetical bond is issued at par (price of 100) with a coupon equal to its current par yield. Using the proceeds method, we then estimate the bond’s forward yield over the target horizon. Carry is defined as the difference between this forward yield and the current par yield of that maturity. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 95 Fundamental Equilibrium Exchange Rate (FEER) Valuations The FEER measure estimates a currency’s fundamental equilibrium exchange rate by identifying the real exchange rate consistent with sustainable current account position of the economy in question. The equilibrium exchange rate are computed both in REER index terms and as implied USD/CCY nominal crosses, providing fair value benchmarks. Use cases We and our clients leverage the FEER valuations to compare spot exchange rates with model-implied fair value, identify which currencies are structurally over- or undervalued, and anchor medium- to long-term forecast endpoints. Because the framework ties currency values to sustainable current-account balances, it can also be used to judge whether market pricing is consistent with external equilibrium, distinguish cyclical overshoots from deeper structural misalignments, and frame scenario analysis around shifts in fiscal policy, productivity, or terms of trade. Comparing the REER-based and USD/CCY versions further helps separate multilateral competitiveness from bilateral dollar positioning, making the series useful for both strategic allocation and trade expression. It is best treated as a strategic anchor rather than a near-term timing signal. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 39 Government Bonds | Seasonally-Adjusted TIPS Real Yields, Breakevens These measures provide constant maturity Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) real yields and inflation breakevens adjusted to remove predictable seasonal patterns in Consumer Price Index (CPI) indexation. Because TIPS principal is linked to CPI through Treasury index ratios, observed breakevens can move for purely seasonal reasons even when the underlying inflation outlook is unchanged. The seasonally-adjusted series strip out those recurring effects and offer a cleaner view of real rate pricing and inflation compensation across maturities. Use cases Investors use these series to compare TIPS valuations across months without mechanically predictable CPI seasonality obscuring the signal. They help separate moves driven by underlying inflation expectations and real rates from moves driven by seasonal carry, especially in the front end of the curve where seasonality matters most. Strategists can use them around CPI releases, auction cycles, and relative-value screens, while portfolio managers and risk managers can use them to assess inflation hedges and scenario outcomes on a seasonally consistent basis. Calculation methodology To get a seasonally adjusted TIPS curve, we fit a Nelson Siegel curve through the seasonally adjusted TIPS yields. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 27 US Treasury Daily Financing Need This measures the Treasury’s daily borrowing requirement based on actual government spending and receipts from the Daily Treasury Statement. It reflects actual financing needs and signals expected issuance of bills and/or coupons. By quantifying short-term funding requirements, it provides a window into how much the Treasury must raise to meet obligations and manage cash balances. Use cases The net deficit measure serves as a high-frequency proxy for Treasury supply pressure. Rising net issuance relative to TGA movements can signal heavier upcoming auction supply, which is directionally bearish for U.S. rates and useful for short-term duration positioning. Tracking day-over-day TGA changes allows rates strategists to infer whether the government is absorbing or injecting liquidity into the banking system. Large TGA drawdowns represent reserve injections, loosening financial conditions, while TGA rebuilds drain reserves — a key input for Fed liquidity analysis. Calculation methodology We compute the net deficit as the difference between the net change in marketable securities and the day-over-day change in the Treasury General Account (TGA) closing balance. The net change in debt outstanding is computed as the difference between gross issuance and redemptions. We use the Daily Treasury Statement (DTS), published by the Fed, as the data source. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 83 Interest Rate Swaps | Carry & Roll Down Swap roll down and carry tickers quantify the expected return components of a swap position under a stable yield curve. Roll down reflects how the par swap rate changes as the position moves toward shorter maturities, while carry captures the return earned from the difference between forward and current swap rates over a given horizon. Together, they provide a structured view of expected swap performance by isolating the effects of time passage and forward curve positioning. This helps investors identify relative value opportunities and optimise curve strategies. Use cases These metrics have similar use cases as defined in the Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Carry & Roll Down. Calculation methodology We calculate swap carry and roll down using the fixed-rate OIS and forward swap curves. Carry measures the return from holding a swap position over a given horizon under a stable curve, while roll down captures the change in rate as the swap “moves down” the curve with time. Carry is computed as the difference between the forward rate of the specified maturity minus the carry period and the current OIS rate of that maturity. Roll down is calculated as the difference between the current rate of the specified maturity and the rate of the same maturity minus the roll down period. Batteries help to provide the one thing required in the system – flexibility. BESS can reduce data centre grid draws by providing an alternative source of energy during periods of high grid stress, especially when paired with on-site generation. BESS can also discharge energy rapidly during power spikes, smoothing the aggregate power consumption even with extreme short-term fluctuations. On-site BESS installations could hence expedite grid connection approvals by easing infrastructure constraints and reducing risks of grid emergencies for utilities. This is especially evident in the US, where policy reforms allow customers to have their grid connection accelerated if they agree to curtailment during high-grid-stress periods. Thermal-BESS pairing: Given long grid connection queues, data centres are increasingly considering on-site thermal generation for power supply as it is usually faster to deploy. BESS is essential in such scenarios as it performs three key functions – protecting equipment, improving plant efficiency and providing grid- forming capabilities. BNEF reported that 1MW of storage (with a two-hour duration) is likely present for every 2MWof on-site power generation. German Q3 issuance outlook update on 25th June We expect the 25th June update to broadly reaffirm the existing 2026 issuance framework, with no change to the headline bond supply anchored to the €98bn borrowing assumption set in December. Once the forward curve is obtained, we compute all significant local maxima and minima and sort them based on their prominence with respect to neighboring points. From this set, at most three of the most prominent peaks and troughs are selected. This approach ensures that a trough always appears between two peaks and vice versa The methodology prioritizes the most relevant turning point first, with prominence used as a secondary criterion. In cases where the curve is monotonic, or when no peak or no trough is identified, the 30-year point is assigned as the corresponding value. The position of each identified peak and trough is also reported through the “months to peak” and “months to trough” tickers, translating turning points into their time horizons along the curve. This provides a consistent and interpretable framework for tracking structural inflection points across different curve shapes. records.text: M Update 2 think it best to compare today's data as a combined April and May reading vs. expectations. We assumed April revisions would leave the decline in payrolls at -10k, with May coming in at -25k. Combined, this would be a -35k drop in headcount. We got a far lesser upward revision in April and a beat in the May reading, all resulting in a 51k drop in payrolls across the two months. We think May data will be revised down, but even absent that, this looks pretty soft and in line with private sector surveys. On the theme of the bifurcation, we note that over the past 12 months, public sector payrolls have risen by 76k, while private sector payrolls have fallen by 195k. This is what fiscal impulse looks in practice - an uplift in government spending from the October 2024 Budget, funded by a payrolls tax hike, delivered an expansion of capacity in the public sector, with a drop in private sector payrolls. Since government spending growth is due to slow sharply into next year, one would expect this dichotomy to close as well. But again, it is fair to say risks are skewed towards a top-up of public sector budgets. In that case, we will keep on seeing similar labour market outcomes as we have this past year. The LFS numbers were much stronger, and entirely driven by self-employment. Per the LFS, self-employment rose by ~170k in the past three months, while employment fell by 70k. For the first time in a long time, it seems like the LFS and HMRC data might be aligned - payrolls

records.text: Balance sheet's mention in the statement On the Fed' balance sheet, we found it noteworthy that the statement reaffirmed the committee's policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. While the details about about policy actions on the balance sheet were left to the FOMC's "implementation note, " we think this sentence was added to mitigate concerns that the FOMC would want to reduce its balance sheet rapidly, given Warsh's longstanding opposition to a large Fed balance sheet. Characterizing both demand and supply changes to the economy In discussing economic conditions, the new statement made some interesting changes, mentioning that activity is expanding at a solid pace, that productivity growth and capital investment are strong, that job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and that the unemployment rate has changed little. The statement notes that inflation remains elevated relative to the 2% goal, in part due to supply shocks. While it continued to comment on activity, job gains, the unemployment rate and inflation, it did insert more supply-side elements, referring to productivity growth, the workforce and supply shocks to inflation. Summary of Economic Projections As we had expected, today's communication included the latest round of economic projections and a fresh dot plot. NZD for instance is projected to see the largest y/y improvement in growth rates relative to last year in DM, and Canadian data is firming as well. But from a top-down perspective, the under- performance is easier to explain. These laggards are cyclical currencies that are sensitive to risk markets and all yielding less than the dollar and hence, it pays investors to be short these currencies vs. USD and have a risk hedge on. Histori- cally, when cyclical currencies have large yield deficits rela- tive to the dollar, they have faced persistent negative returns when the rate differential is relatively range-bound, which can compound over time. records.text: 4) “Going Global” is still ongoing Sustained momentum: Chinese corporate overseas revenue exposure continued n its upward trajectory to 18% in 2025 from 16% in 2024. The Auto sector has been the leader of this globalization trend, surging to 29% in 2025 (+8pp vs. 2024 due to rapid EV overseas expansion), and the 1Q26 results for the sector leader confirmed the trend. This globalization trend is increasingly broad-based, with Semiconductors, Transportation, Capital Goods, Durables, and Pharma & Biotech also making inroads. Conversely, Tech Hardware (driven by smartphones) and Energy both declined. Profitability premium: Most sectors still enjoy better profit margins in overseas n markets compared to their domestic operations (as shown in Exhibit 16), providing a strong structural incentive for continued international expansion. In fact, Chinese exporters (>50% overseas exposure) delivered robust growth across both revenue and earnings in 1Q26 (see Exhibit 28 in Appendix), significantly higher than the aggregate listed universe. FX impact: The FX impact reversed to a net loss of Rmb5.8bn in 2025 from a net n gain of Rmb3.3bn in 2024, driven by a slight appreciation of the CNY against the USD (on a full-year average basis). Export-heavy and commodity-related segments (including Industrials, Materials, Energy, and IT) experienced a squeeze, while USD-debt-heavy sectors (such as Airlines) and Consumer Discretionary capitalized on this currency strength. 21 June 2026 7 Goldman Sach

records.text: ebt. On the positive side, copper and lithium revenues provide a meaningful cushion to the government’s base case. The 2026 budget was built on conservative commodity assumptions, with copper priced around USD5.20/lb compared to current USD6.00/lb. Wider fiscal deficit and Kast’s reform test Each additional dollar per pound of copper adds roughly 0.5pp of fiscal revenue as a share of GDP; if copper prices remain near current levels, the effective deficit could be 0.3−0.5pp lower than the government’s base- case figure. Kast’s reform agenda: President José Antonio Kast’s economic program seeks to revive private investment by accelerating environmental and permitting approvals for large projects; cutting the corporate income-tax rate from 27% to 23%; and reforming the pension system to improve adequacy while offering greater individual-account flexibility. The April 2026 reconstruction package contains more than 40 measures across these pillars. Congressional approval has been challenging. The governing coalition holds only 25 of the 50 Senate seats, and several moderate right-wing senators have expressed reservations about the pace and scope of fiscal consolidation. The corporate-tax-cut component faces opposition from centre-left senators who view it as regressive. We therefore anticipate diluted versions of the main reforms to pass over 2026–27, with the full implementation of President Kast’s corporate-tax reduction reform unlikely before 2028. Calculation methodology We estimate FEER with country-level ARDL regressions that relate smoothed quarterly REERs to the current account, fiscal balance, net foreign asset position, relative productivity, and terms of trade, allowing for dynamic lag structures and persistence in exchange-rate behavior. Inputs are standardized to quarterly frequency, with REER first smoothed through a 12-month rolling mean and current-account-to-GDP measures converted to four-quarter rolling sums to reduce seasonal and transitory noise. The model uses IMF's External Balance Assessment current-account (EBA-CA) norms serve as proxies for sustainable current account positions; substituting those norms into the estimated equations yields equilibrium REER values. Those REER-based fair values are then translated into USD/CCY valuations through a trade-weighted system of bilateral misalignments with a USD consistency constraint. The latest fair value is then marked-to- market to compare the fair-value estimate with the latest monthly REER and spot cross. (see Assessing Fair Value in FX: A FEER Approach). records.text: Importantly, European natural gas pricing has remained relatively in check in face of what has been one of the largest gas supply shocks in history, suggesting the market is comfortable with this estimated storage fill - otherwise we would have seen higher European gas prices, in order to disincentive LNG demand outside of Europe and, in turn, drive LNG supply into Europe higher than it has been. We believe this lower NW European storage target vs history – the four-year pre-energy crisis average storage fill was 88% - is consistent with a significant rise in LNG imports and a structural drop in European gas demand since the 2022 energy crisis. To be sure, total winter supply availability in Europe is still down vs the pre-energy-crisis average, even if that drop has been significantly moderated by rising European LNG imports in the period (Exhibit 2). But demand has dropped more. The 2022 European energy crisis triggered a pick up in heat-pump installations, which reduced residential heating demand in the winter, and the lasting curtailment of energy-intensive industrial activity, which also weighed on industrial demand for power. That led to a large, sticky drop in European natural gas demand (Exhibit 3, Exhibit 4). We assess the extent of the competitiveness decoupling with the Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) indicator from the OECD, which can be interpreted as a measure of specialization in a given product market. • An RCA value of +1 indicates that a particular country “c” is the sole global exporter of a particular product “p”, while a value of -1 means that the country does not export the product at all. A value of 0 indicates that the country's export share is identical to the product's global trade share. Positive values suggest a comparative advantage, as the country's export share exceeds the share of the product in global trade. • This left-hand chart plots the RCA for both the EU and China across more than 5,600 distinct product categories. Each dot represents a single product. • By analyzing the position and movement of these products, as well as the shape of the scatter over time, we: i) identify product markets in which the EU and China are direct competitors (top right quadrant), ii) assess areas of clear dominance for each bloc. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 5 Market Prices by Time Zone We track intraday price movements across different trading periods. The goal is to have tickers representing the daily moves in global assets/rates during Tokyo, London, and New York trading to help us identify drivers or patterns in price movements. Use cases We use regional price segmentation to study intraday liquidity, identify geographic centers of price discovery (including supply and demand), and analyze spillovers across trading sessions. Portfolio managers apply the data to monitor cross-region execution costs. Macro researchers employ the series to isolate time-zone-specific shocks, while risk managers use it to test how liquidity fragmentation affects valuation under scenarios. Calculation methodology We calculate a cumulative sum of the daily moves in four time zones in order to split the nearly 24-hour trading session into its major market components. We define a daily move as occurring from the close of preceding time zone session close to close of time zone in question. We define the Tokyo time zone from 7 PM to 3 AM New York time, London from 3 AM to 8 AM New York time, New York Morning from 8 AM to 1 PM New York time, and New York Afternoon from 1 PM to 5 PM New York time. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Global Macro Strategy Bloomberg Consensus Year-Ahead Forecasts This measure tracks daily revisions to Bloomberg consensus one-year-ahead forecasts for key macro variables, including real GDP growth, CPI inflation, the unemployment rate, and the budget balance. By focusing on a rolling year-ahead horizon rather than a single calendar-year estimate, the series are designed to show how economist expectations evolve through time in a way that is more comparable across dates and countries. Use cases Investors use these series to monitor revision momentum in the macro outlook and to distinguish changes in consensus from the level of the forecast itself. Rates and FX strategists can compare growth and inflation revisions across countries when interpreting curve repricing, central-bank expectations, and relative-currency moves. The series are also useful for event studies around data releases and policy meetings, for judging how quickly economists incorporate new information, and for identifying where market pricing may be moving ahead of or lagging the consensus. Calculation methodology We use Bloomberg survey consensus forecasts for the annual macro variables included in the Almanac. To construct a rolling one-year-ahead measure, we linearly interpolate between adjacent calendar-year forecasts based on the share of the next twelve months falling in each year. lowering the consumption tax on food, a move that will be closely watched. The National Council on Social Security submitted a plan on 17 June to cut the tax rate on food products to 1% as a temporary measure until the government launches a refundable tax credit. This, coupled with benefits for low- and medium-income earners, would effectively reduce the tax to zero. However, it is far from certain whether this proposal will gain support from either the LDP or opposition parties. The biggest problem is how to finance the estimated annual revenue shortfall of around ¥5trn. (The financial burden will increase further if proposed subsidies for agriculture and the restaurant industry are implemented.) Corporate subsidies and revisions to special tax measures alone are far from sufficient, and one suggestion that has emerged is to use any tax revenue overruns. That, though, relies on growth in nominal tax revenues from inflation, a policy contradiction since it could indirectly exacerbate the very inflation it is supposed to fight. We believe the markets will be highly sensitive to news flow related to fiscal and tax policy over the coming two weeks, including discussions over a consumption tax cut and any new growth strategies that may be announced at the same time. records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research ❑ Key takeaways: ❑ The EU trade deficit with China has widened to around EUR370bn, close to a record high (2% of GDP). Machinery and transport equipment explain c.60% of the deficit. Goods imports from China had temporarily surged during the pandemic lockdowns, but imports are back on their rising long-term trend. More worrying is that Europe’s exports to China have begun to decline. ❑ Price competitiveness is playing a key role, and subsides are supporting China’s advantage. The PPI differential moved markedly in China’s favour after the Ukraine-invasion shocked European energy costs. China’s ‘anti-involution’ policy might be stabilizing the PPI differential, but the gap remains wide. Chinese subsidies have helped push down Chinese producer prices, and we show the correlation between the scale of subsidies and market share gains by China. ❑ Using product-level data, we demonstrate the evolution to more direct competition between the EU and China. We do this with the Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) index to compare EU and Chinese exports across more than 5,600 product categories. We find a high concentration of products in which both economies have a comparative advantage, that is, direct competition. ❑ Europe remains competitive, but China’s dominance is beginning to grow. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 75 Government Bonds | STRIPS Outstanding and WAM We quantify the U.S. Treasury Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities (STRIPS) market by separately reporting outstanding balances and weighted- average maturity (WAM) for principal STRIPS and coupon STRIPS. By decomposing zero- coupon supply into its principal and coupon components, it provides a clean view of duration supply across maturities, facilitating comparisons with coupon-bearing issuance and clarifying how stripping/reattachment activity reshapes the term structure of investable government duration. Use cases Investors and traders track the amount of outstanding STRIPS versus outstanding coupon supply to gauge duration demand, especially from insurance and pension funds, a main user of STRIPS. CUSIP-level stripping flows can also show additional duration demand in key sectors of the curve. Calculation methodology Using the Treasury's MSPD and the CUSIP-level data on the amount of a security outstanding, we take the cash flows of all stripped bonds and calculate the outstanding balance of C-strips and P-strips. By then weighting and adjusting for the maturity dates of the stripped cash flows, we also calculate the weighted-average maturity (WAM) of the strips universe. records.text: 2 Euro Area Viewpoint | 18 June 2026 Economics What is the mandate; what is the target? The ECB’s main objective, enshrined in Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), is to maintain price stability. There is a small top-up: “Without prejudice to this objective, the ECB shall also support the general economic policies of the European Union”. The definition of “price stability” is the responsibility of the ECB itself. Since the 2020/21 strategy review, the ECB has a symmetric inflation target of 2% in the medium term (typically assumed to be a 2-3-year horizon). It was previously asymmetric – i.e., “inflation close to but below 2%”. The inflation target is now symmetric on paper – i.e., tolerating upward and downward deviations alike. But actual policy decisions over the past few years suggest to us a slight preference for sub-2%, still. That contrasts with the more flexible approach of the Bank of England, for instance. The ECB’s monetary policy framework says it targets Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) inflation, but the focus remains on both headline and core – i.e., excluding energy and food. Owner-occupied housing costs enter into policy considerations indirectly, too. Who takes monetary policy decisions? The ECB Governing Council consists of six Executive Board members (including the President) and the 21 national central bank governors of Euro area member states. records.text: Balance Sheet Task Force On balance sheet, two aspects of the FOMC meeting stand out. First, Chair Warsh announced a task force on balance sheet policy “to review the benefits and risks of the current ample reserves regime and the composition of the balance sheet. ” Second, the policy statement included language that the Committee “reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. ” At first glance, these developments may appear at odds. In practice, they point to a straightforward sequencing: the status quo remains in place unless and until the review leads to changes in the framework. Put differently, the Fed is unlikely to transition away from the current regime before a clear alternative is established. That said, the Fed has already been through a review of the implementation framework, it looked broadly at different regimes before it decided on ample. The task force itself should not come as a surprise given Chair Warsh’s longstanding hawkish tilt on the balance sheet. Beyond the announcement of the review, there were few details on which direction the chairman himself is leaning. What changes could emerge from this review? The most obvious alternative would be a return to a scarce reserves regime, in which the policy rate is determined more directly by the supply of reserves. records.text: 3) Recovering aggregate revenues but bifurcated margins in “involuted” sectors Revenue acceleration: In 1Q26, the aggregate revenue growth for the listed n universe picked up to +4% yoy, up from +1% in 2025 and -1% in 2024. This overall improvement masks a bifurcated sector landscape, characterized by sharp rebounds in cyclicals and tech-heavy sectors (Brokers/IT/Industrial all +15% yoy in 1Q26), a stabilization in consumer staples, and substantial declines in Real Estate. Margin divergence: The net margin for the listed universe remained stable, ticking n up slightly to 9.0% in 1Q26 (from 8.9% in 1Q25). Consumer-facing New Economy/POE and Banks (pressured by narrowing NIM) generally underperformed their Old Economy/SOE counterparts. Among our defined “involuted” sectors, Semiconductors, Industrial Metals, and Airlines (aided by an 8% yoy decline in domestic jet fuel prices in 1Q26) were the primary margin gainers. Conversely, the margin erosion was exacerbated in select consumer sectors (Autos, Agriculture, and E-commerce), Construction Materials (such as Cement and Steel) and Solar Equipment, highlighting a stark divergence between a hard-tech recovery and a consumer/property-linked slowdown. See Exhibit 33 in Appendix for more details. records.text: onsists of six Executive Board members (including the President) and the 21 national central bank governors of Euro area member states. The board members are appointed for single, eight-year mandates by the European Council, following consultations with the European Parliament and the Governing Council. Typically, nominations to the ECB Executive Board are part of a broader “big EU jobs” allocation discussion across EU/Euro area member states. The next three mandates coming to term are those of Chief Economist Lane (May 2027), President Lagarde (October 2027) and Schnabel, responsible for market operations (December 27). National central bank governors are appointed according to varying national procedures. How can 27 Governing Council members come to a decision? In theory, the Governing Council follows a voting rotation: the six Executive Board members vote at all times, the national central bank governors of the five largest members share four voting rights, and all the others share 11 voting rights, with a monthly rotation. We would refrain from spending much time on the rotation schedule. It’s a technical detail, with no tangible implication for policy outcomes, in our view. The chief economist presents a proposed policy decision, and all Governing Council members participate in the discussions. What next? Absent a renewed near-term spike in commodity prices, the July MPR should bring a material downward revision to the near-term inflation path, with the Bank's inflation expectations-based models thus likely revising even the medium- term forecasts down a touch. H2 issuance: 10yr supply to dominate Q3, peak NCR in July Under an unchanged 2026 bond issuance programme as outlined in December, Q3 should see elevated bond supply (€95–99bn), before a seasonal slowdown in Q4 (€61-65bn) – see weekly supply monitor for detailed breakdown. Q3 supply dynamics is characterized by a strong pivot toward the 10yr sector and front - loaded net cash requirements (NCR). 10y Bunds are set to dominate Q3 issuance ( ~ 31% share, Figure 13 ) - the highest Q3 allocation since 2022. Long-end issuance (10yr+) is expected to rebalance, with the share of 30yr declining from Q2 into Q3– Q4, though still exceeding the 15–20yr segment, consistent with expectations of a further 30y syndication in September. In terms of NCR, Q3 should account for 30% of annual NCR ( ~60bn), with July the peak month, contributing nearly half of Q3 and marking the strongest NCR in H2 (Figure 14). This is in line with the methodology described in Dallas Fed President Logan’s speech this past February. After the Fed cut policy rates to 5.25% in 1996, policy rates were still ~75-100bp above the Fed’s neutral rate estimate–still in restrictive territory. Conversely, after 175bp of cumulative cuts in late 2024 (100bp) and late 2025 (75bp), policy rates in the US are closer to the Fed’s estimate of neutral, as evidenced in Figure 2P o l i c y r a t e s i n t h e U S a r e c l o s e r t o t h e F e d ’ s e s t i m a t e s o f n e u t r a l . The implication of this historical analysis is that the bar for cutting is high: Chair Greenspan could afford patience at a more-restrictive starting point, while the current Fed’s patience has a tighter margin for error. The lack of a clear signal in productivity data will remain, limiting the Fed’s ability to cut rates in a world where the economy remains strong, inflation remains sticky and the labour market is improving, as in our baseline. Moreover, with policy rates already close to the broad neutral level, there is limited room for error. Over time, alternative data may suggest that some productivity gains are in the pipeline; however, we believe that new Fed Chair Warsh will find it difficult to convince the FOMC to ease preventively in anticipation of the productivity gains that are yet to be seen. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 73 Government Bonds | Dealer Holdings as % of ex-SOMA Primary dealer holdings, expressed as a share of total outstanding Treasury securities excluding Federal Reserve SOMA balances, provide a clear view of dealer participation in sovereign debt markets. The measure highlights how much of the ex-SOMA Treasury supply resides on dealer balance sheets, reflecting inventory levels, balance sheet utilization, and market-making capacity. Use cases Investors use this measure to monitor how much Treasury supply dealers are warehousing on their balance sheets and to identify where absorption is concentrated across the curve. Strategists use it to assess dealer participation, market-making capacity, balance sheet pressure, and the risk of liquidity strains in specific maturity sectors. Calculation methodology We compute the ratio of primary dealer holdings, based on regulatory submissions, to total Treasury securities outstanding after excluding SOMA balances. Outstanding amounts are sourced from official Treasury data. The resulting ratio provides a liquidity- adjusted measure of primary dealer participation, consistent with established balance sheet and market structure monitoring practices. records.text: bearish tail risk hedge Gilt yields are modestly lower over the week with the front end of the US curve underper- forming (Figure 1G i l t y i e l d s a r e m o d e s t l y l o w e r o n t h e w e e k w i t h t h e f r o n t e n d o f t h e U S c u r v e u n d e r p e r f o r m i n g f o l l o w i n g t h e h a w k i s h F e d d e l i v e r y ) on a more hawkish Fed delivery. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 63 Government Bonds | Yield Spread to Spline This measure evaluates the difference between observed government bond yields and a fitted spline curve, aggregated across maturities. The spline serves as a smooth benchmark for curve dynamics. Yield spreads to spline highlight deviations from expected structure, indicating relative value opportunities or dislocations in sovereign debt markets that might otherwise remain hidden in raw yield data. Use cases Investors and portfolio managers use aggregate spline spreads to spot broad curve dislocations and mispricings. Strategists and traders can apply it when analyzing issuance impacts and to identify market regimes and opportunities from a liquidity and relative valuation perspective. Calculation methodology We begin with the discount curve produced by the Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Par/Spot Yields framework . This curve provides discount factors across the relevant maturity spectrum and represents the model-implied term structure used to value future cash flows. For each bond, we construct the remaining cash-flow schedule, including coupon payments and principal repayment. Each cash flow is discounted using the model-implied discount factor corresponding to its payment date. Finally, we compute the mean absolute error across all eligible bonds with maturities greater than one year. A lower MAE indicates that the fitted discount curve more closely matches observed market yield

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 71 Government Bonds | Weekly Issuance | Net DV01 This measure calculates the net DV01 added by government bond issuance after accounting for securities maturing or being redeemed. It represents the incremental interest rate risk introduced into the market each week. By balancing gross issuance against maturities, the measure isolates true additions to systemic sensitivity and provides a clearer picture of supply-demand dynamics. Use cases Investors track net DV01 to gauge whether issuance meaningfully increases market risk exposure. Portfolio managers incorporate it when projecting yield pressures from government bond supply. Strategists compare it against demand indicators to assess absorption capacity. Risk managers rely on net rather than gross DV01 for stress testing because it reflects actual additions to outstanding rate risk. Calculation methodology We calculate net DV01 as gross issuance DV01 minus the DV01 of coupon payments plus the DV01 of QE/QT. This produces the incremental interest rate risk added to the system by net supply. This calculation aligns with flow-based debt sustainability models, providing an accurate measure of Treasury-driven changes in systemic duration exposure. The uploaded values are in US dollar terms by default, however, a toggle allows users to use it in local currency terms. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 99 EM Sovereign Credit Spreads by Rating This measure tracks representative emerging-market sovereign credit spreads for broad rating buckets ranging from AA to CCC. By grouping sovereign spread levels by credit quality, it provides a daily view of how investors are pricing default risk, refinancing risk, and external vulnerability across the EM credit spectrum. The series offer a clean summary of the level and shape of EM sovereign risk premia, helping users separate broad beta moves from changes concentrated in specific quality tiers. Use cases Investors use these series to compare value across EM rating buckets, monitor whether spread moves are concentrated in higher-beta or higher-quality sovereigns, and judge whether broader market repricing is being driven by global risk sentiment or by deterioration lower in the quality stack. Portfolio managers can use them as benchmark hurdle rates for country allocation and relative-value work, while strategists can track dispersion across rating buckets as a signal of stress, contagion, or improving market access across EM sovereigns. Calculation methodology We group a broad EM sovereign universe into the Bloomberg rating buckets shown in the Almanac—AA, A, BBB, BB, B, and CCC—and assign each sovereign to the relevant bucket using its prevailing composite rating. The most recent example is 2022, when Mélenchon was polling around 18% but ended up claiming 22% of votes, just 1pp short of proceeding to the second round. What about the second round? The few simulations available so far show that Bardella would win against Mélenchon with two-thirds of votes (Exhibit 3). Polls suggest that he would also win against Glucksmann, Attal, and Retailleau, with 55-60% of votes. But a potential contest between Bardella and Philippe would result in a closer race, with polls currently averaging to a toss-up. Prediction markets ascribe a significantly higher probability to a win for Bardella (26%) rather than Le Pen (8%), although she remains the party’s official candidate (Exhibit 4). We continue to expect a prolonged hold before cuts in 2027 Overall, we continue to expect the next policy move to be a cut (in February and April 2027), not a hike, in contrast to market pricing for more than one hike (+30.3bp) by year-end. Given the weak starting point of the economy, including the labour market, the more limited and targeted fiscal response as well as a still-restrictive policy rate (3.75%), we believe that the Bank can address the risk of second-round effects by keeping rates at the current restrictive level for longer, without hiking them further. That said, we acknowledge the Committee's hawkish bias, as was made clear today, hence, leaving the door open to rate hikes. However, even in a scenario in which the MPC were to hike rates, the weaker starting point for the economy would, in our view, imply a relatively rapid reversal via rate cuts thereafter. So while we do not rule out BoE rate hikes, we continue to see them as a risk scenario rather than the base case. OIS contracts: a direct gauge of ECB expectations The reference floating rate for OIS contracts is the euro short-term rate (€STR), which reflects the wholesale euro unsecured overnight borrowing costs of banks located in the euro area. It is calculated and published daily by the ECB, based on confidential statics on money market transactions reported by a total of now 69 banks. €STR follows closely the ECB Deposit rate. It currently fixes at a spread of around -7bp below the Depo rate. That spread has evolved in a -10 to -5bp range in the past 5 years, depending on excess liquidity. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 93 DXY Index Excluding Individual Components The indexes consist of modified versions of the US Dollar Index in which each of the six component currencies is excluded in turn. By removing one currency from the trade- weighted basket, these indexes isolate the contribution of each bilateral exchange rate to overall DXY performance while preserving the index methodology. Use cases Investors use these indexes to decompose the drivers of dollar strength or weakness. By comparing the full DXY against versions excluding EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD, SEK, or CHF, analysts identify which crosses account for observed movements. Portfolio managers employ them for attribution analysis, relative value trades, and as benchmarks when constructing hedges against non-US currencies. Calculation methodology We recalculate the DXY index by excluding one currency from the basket and renormalizing the weights of the remaining components proportionally to their original shares. The index is computed as the geometric mean of the adjusted bilateral rates relative to the base year (1973 = 100). Each variant follows the standard DXY formula with modified currency composition. Data-centre infrastructure is undoubtedly copper-intensive, but we think market expectations have become far too aggressive . This has perhaps been fuelled by an error in an Nvidia publication in January which had initially stated that a 1GW facility would require 500,000 tonnes of copper for server rack architecture alone. Given total global installation was 14.9GW, last year, this would suggest 7.5 Mt of copper demand. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 19 Shadow Monetary Policy Rates Shadow monetary policy rates, or shadow short rates (SSRs), estimate the overnight policy rate implied if central banks had relied solely on negative interest rates rather than unconventional measures such as QE or forward guidance. They adjust observed yield curves to account for the option to hold cash, providing a counterfactual rate that quantifies the level of monetary policy rates. Use cases Investors use SSRs to compare monetary policy across economies constrained by the effective lower bound. SSR differentials explain currency movements more reliably than nominal short-rate differentials and serve as inputs in FX forecasting models. Analysts monitor SSRs to quantify unconventional stimulus in conventional terms, anticipate cross- market policy divergence, and assess the effectiveness of QE or guidance programs. Calculation methodology We estimate SSRs using the Krippner two-factor affine Nelson–Siegel model with an option-adjusted term structure. Zero-coupon OIS curves provide input yields. The model incorporates a lower-bound constraint by pricing bonds as options: constrained yields equal unconstrained forward rates minus the option value of holding cash. The shadow short rate corresponds to the shortest point on the unconstrained forward curve (see Shadow Short Rates For G10 FX). records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS Summer Shines. A combination of World Cup optimism and the confirmation of a US –Iran peace deal provides a timely lift for Asia after a challenging three months. Since the onset of the conflict, Asia n currencies have depreciated by an average of -2.3% amid concerns over oil supply disruptions and rising inflation expectations (Figure 2). The impact has been most acute in South Asia given its heavy reliance on oil imports, while aggressive foreign outflows also weighed on KRW and IDR. Encouragingly, investors are beginning to return, with 20-day FX flows turning back into net inflows across North Asia. While oil price normalization may take time even post -deal, Asian central banks appear far more calibrated in their response compared to the post-COVID period, showing a clear reluctance to overreact to transitory inflation shocks (Figure 3). With limited pass-through from oil into aggregate inflation, we expect policy rates to remain broadly aligned with current market pricing, as policymakers prioritize growth over prices. At the same time, we recognize recent Asian FX underperformance has been driven more by higher US yields and uncertainty around the Fed’s policy path (Figure 4). As inflation expectations begin to mean-revert, these external headwinds should gradually fade, providing fresh support for Asia. Portfolio Change. Our Asia strategy has focused on relative value trades, favoring resilient North As

Against this, we see some mitigating factors: 1) EM fundamentals are in good shape overall and hence perhaps the judgment of the starting point of carry needs to be ‘quality’ adjusted. EM real yields currently com- pensate well for BoP positions and are consistent with posi- tive FX returns. 2) Several EM central banks have scope to be proactive with hikes supported by resilient growth. 3) Fed policy rate hikes also have to be judged against the outlook for US inflation. We find that EM FX tends to unavoidably sell-off during periods of fast Fed repricing, but a more per- sistent negative outlook arises when the US rate shift is led by real yields rather than breakeven rates. This unfavorable real/ breakeven combination has dominated since early May. How- ever, we are yet to learn if the Fed’s reaction function is turn- ing more hawkish or only responsive to higher inflation. • EM FX: We returned to an OW stance in EM FX with a preference for high yielders (see here). However, Policy Board member T oichiro Asada did vote against the hike, strongly suggesting dovishness on the part of the Takaichi government. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 25 Commodity Trading Advisor (CTA) | Flows This measure estimates buying or selling activity generated by CTAs as momentum signals change. It projects flows that systematic strategies are likely to execute, based on returns and positioning models. Because CTAs follow rules-based systems, their adjustments can create measurable and predictable pressures on asset prices, particularly during periods of heightened volatility or market reversals. Use cases Investors monitor CTA flows to anticipate trading pressure and potential liquidity effects in major asset classes. They use it to prepare for flow-driven volatility and to recognize when systematic traders could amplify directional moves. Risk managers could incorporate expected CTA flows into short-term stress testing frameworks. Calculation methodology We compute flows as the change in estimated CTA holdings implied by evolving trend signals. We assume a two-day lag between signal generation and execution. Forecasts extend asset price paths flat or under stress scenarios. We calculate flows as the delta in units held, scaled by assumed AUM, producing predicted directional liquidity effects (see Understanding CTA Positioning And Forecasting CTA Flows). Real wages are still expanding at a 3-4 % y/y rate, but we expect the pace to ease to around 2 % by the end of 2026 as the cadence of minimum-wage adjustments slows and the mandated reduction in weekly hours begins to dent per-worker earnings in certain industries. Given a weaker-than-anticipated carry-over for the year, a slower rebound in supply-driven sectors, and an expected deceleration in income growth, we anticipate weaker private-consumption support. Consequently, we lower our 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.6 % from the previous 2.4 %. Despite the modest start, we still expect investment to rise as the Kast administration pushes to unlock the investment pipeline. Data from the Chilean Capital Goods Corporation show that private investment—both realised and pipeline—will total roughly USD 70 bn between 2026 and 2030, led by mining (USD 30 bn in copper and lithium), energy (USD 17 bn in renewables), public works (USD 10 bn) and housing (USD 6 bn). Private investment in Q1 2026 alone amounted to an annualised USD 70 bn, still below the 2010-14 average of USD 78 bn but comfortably above the post-2018 trough of USD 42 bn. We are not revising the assumption of higher investment, but merely postponing the onset of its effects in the data. For these reasons we keep our 2027 GDP growth projection at 3.0 %. records.text: M Update 2 Philadelphia Manufacturing Activity Reinforces Momentum Manufacturing activity was strong in June, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia’s Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey. The headline general business activity diffusion index rose 10.7 points to 10.3 in June, around the same as its 6-month average of 10.8. Demand and production showed strength. The shipments index grew 10 points to 14.9, marking a seventh consecutive month of growth. Meanwhile, the new orders index increased 29 points to 27.3, pointing to strong demand. We think the weakness in the May new orders index was a moderation from a very strong April, the incoming June data reinforce the continuous momentum in manufacturing demand. Labor demand from manufacturers showed signs of improvement. The employment index grew to 7.9 from -2.8, yet the average workweek index fell to -6.5 from 1.2. Supply chain & inventories: delivery times shortened substantially. The delivery times index moved up to -2.6 from -10.4, meaningfully lower than its averages of 5.4 and 1.2 in 1Q26 and 4Q25. Inventories decreased, with the index falling 15.1 points to -8.5. Prices: prices paid accelerated whereas prices received decelerated. Both indices were meaningfully higher than where they were two years ago. We published our own proprietary dbDataInsights household inflation expectation for May earlier in the month (the data is released around a month before the ECB's data). This series has done a reasonable job so far tracking the changes in CES expectation since the start of the war. Our May dbDataInsights survey showed that after having risen sharply in March, and remaining elevated in April, long-term inflation expectations unwound around half the energy shock in May (2.09% vs 1.9% in February before the war, and 2.26% in March and April). records.text: ation surprises. Aggregate DM and EM versions of these series serve as broad measures of global inflation pressure. To build the 1M aggregates, we normalize each region’s monthly (quarterly) surprises over the prior 12 months (four quarters) by dividing each by the standard deviation of surprises across those periods. We then create daily normalized series by assigning each date the standardized surprise available between data releases, rather than specific to the month or quarter. Wednesday’s FOMC injected new life into the possibility of n a series of rate hikes for a market that had been consolidating around a less severe inflation outcome. Our economists see an increased risk of hikes later this year but have maintained their baseline that the FOMC will leave the policy rate unchanged through the course of the year. What had been previously diffuse hike pricing has shifted in, with the market pricing nearly two hikes to the Mar/Apr-27 meeting peak in the OIS curve. While that risk is now more front-loaded, the rates curve has not priced a significantly higher peak than the one seen on the heels of the May labor market report (Exhibit 1). As we have observed in other markets, to the extent that the policy reaction function is seen as sufficiently front-footed, greater right tail risk around the very front-end can keep a lid on risk premia further out the curve. This dynamic is visible in the flattening that alongside taking hike pricing to levels consistent with a plausible “insurance” amount has pushed longer-term forwards to levels that are now rich to fair. records.text: , where the bond settles at future horizon n and matures at n+m. The calculation follows the no-arbitrage principle. The value of the forward-starting bond’s coupon and principal cash flows, discounted using the prevailing discount curve, must equal par at the forward settlement date. Equivalently, the discount factor at the forward horizon n is set equal to the discounted value of all future coupon payments and the principal repayment at maturity n+m. The coupon rate that satisfies this condition is the implied par forward yield. records.text: ab 18 June 2026 Global Research UK Economic Comment BoE: On hold; the door to hikes still open BoE keeps rates unchanged in a 7-2 vote As firmly expected, the BoE left the Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% in a 7-2 vote, also in line with expectations. The Committee reiterated its previous message that it “stands ready to act as necessary to ensure that CPI inflation remains on track to meet the 2% target in the medium term”, with all members agreeing that the policy response will depend on the extent of second-round effects. In their individual paragraphs, the majority of the MPC members acknowledged that recent data provided some further evidence that underlying disinflation had been on track before the start of the conflict. However, Governor Bailey’s comments that "risks to inflation and interest rates are on the upside" and that he “would respond promptly” to any signals of second-round effects, point to a hawkish bias. As expected, Megan Greene joined Huw Pill in voting for a hike. In her paragraph, Ms Greene justified her vote as a risk-management approach, arguing that the risk of tightening policy too slowly outweighs the potential negative impact on the economy from a pre-emptive hike. Overall, the meeting delivered no major surprises: the Bank remains data-dependent but continues to signal that further rate increases remain a possibility. Selectively long USD skews with Fed poten- tially in play As a bloc, USD/G10 risk-reversals have understandably not performed through most of 1H26, barring a short-lived period in March around the abrupt onset of the Iran conflict when ex-ante delta positioning was lopsidedly short USDs and ripe for a volatile washout. Both risk-reversal levels and cash USD positions are now better adjusted to the reality of higher oil and UST yields since then, such that a similar deer-in-the- headlights moment is unlikely to repeat barring a realization of tail scenarios on oil. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 67 Government Bonds | Vol-Adjusted Yield Moves This measure tracks volatility-adjusted yield changes for constant-maturity government bond yields across major developed markets. It converts daily or weekly yield moves into standardized z-score-like measures by dividing the yield change by its recent historical volatility, helping users compare the size of yield moves across countries and maturities. Use cases The primary use case is identifying when a market has experienced an unusually large or small move relative to its own history, independent of its absolute volatility level. It provides a standardised way to score the market impact of macro events across history. This consistent framework enables backtesting of event-driven strategies using comparable units. Traders can use them to flag rich or cheap curve points after outsized moves, while strategists can monitor whether repricing is concentrated in specific countries or maturities, or across the broader global rates complex. Calculation methodology For each country, we use par yields across maturities from 1Y to 30Y and calculate daily yield changes in basis points, divided by a 90-business-day rolling standard deviation of daily changes. Weekly yield changes are calculated from Thursday observations, using the latest available prior value when Thursday data are missing, and divided by a 52-week rolling standard deviation. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 31 Interest Rate Strategy Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Par/Spot Yields This measure provides government bond yields interpolated to constant maturities in par and spot formats. Par yields represent coupon-bearing bonds priced at par, while spot yields represent zero-coupon equivalents. It establishes standardized benchmarks across maturities, enabling consistent comparison and analysis of yield levels and curve dynamics independent of specific security issuance dates. Use cases Investors use par and spot curves for valuation, curve fitting, and risk analysis. They support decisions about duration management and the shape of the yield curve. Traders rely on them to identify arbitrage opportunities, while strategists apply them to decompose yield movements into policy rate expectations, term premiums, and longer- term market factors. Calculation methodology The input bond data are preprocessed to remove any outliers to avoid any distortions on the curve arising from the liquidity perspective. The filtered bond data are then assigned a fitting weights through a weighting function that governs each bonds relative influence in the spline estimation, ensuring liquid benchmark bonds are emphasized over the illiquid ones. The filtered and weighted bonds is passed to a Cubic Spline model with pre-defined knot points – which define the structural breakpoints of the fitted curve. records.text: to mean-revert, these external headwinds should gradually fade, providing fresh support for Asia. Portfolio Change. Our Asia strategy has focused on relative value trades, favoring resilient North Asia over more vulnerable South Asia. However, with headwinds beginning to fade and South Asian central banks actively managing currency volatility, we see a diminishing asymmetry and are closing our long CNH/INR position. We expect a gradual return of foreign inflows into the region, which should help stabilize previously pressured South Asian FX. While we continue to favor CNH on valuation and positioning grounds, its upside is likely to be more measured in a weaker USD environment given the PBoC’s preference for controlled, low-volatility appreciation. In contrast, we retain our long TWD/IDR position irrespective of the peace deal. Improving risk sentiment and the persistent surge in Taiwanese exports has historically translated into stronger equities, with positive spillovers into the TWD. This can be seen as a natural adjustment, given the growing risk that underlying inflation will exceed 2%. Looking back, we recall that the consensus among economists until the end of the negative interest rate policy in March 2024 was that rates would remain low for a prolonged period even after the policy was scrapped. However, they raised their forecasts in the face of the BoJ's post-exit communications (i.e., its continued adjustments in the degree of easing) and its surprise rate hike in July of that year. The forecasts subsequently remained stable, but we believe the escalating tensions in the Middle East have triggered a second round of upward revisions. Given the lack of clarity over the BoJ’s future stance and the propensity of economists to be influenced by past trends, we see a strong likelihood of further gradual upward revisions in the consensus forecast in line with actual inflation trends. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 77 Government Bonds | UST Futures Model Outputs These measures are a result of our futures model, which produces risk metrics and option values of US Treasury futures. Comparing model outputs to current market conditions also yields relative value metrics. The model revolves around finding the bonds most likely to become the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) for each futures contract. These values provides insight into relative value distortions and arbitrage opportunities within one of the most liquid fixed-income markets. Use cases Investors use net basis and model outputs to identify arbitrage opportunities between futures and cash bonds. Traders track it to guide decisions on rolling contracts and selecting cheapest-to-deliver securities. Strategists rely on it to monitor demand for hedging through futures, while risk managers incorporate it into valuation models to ensure pricing aligns with carry-adjusted theoretical relationships. Calculation methodology Our model is built around valuing the options built into the futures contracts. To value the quality option, we shock the futures bond basket using historic yield move patterns, measure changes in the CTD bond, and calculate expected changes of the contract. Different parts of this process allow for the calculation of our different model outputs. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 43 Government Bonds | Weighted-Average Yield Weighted-average yield (WAY) measures the portfolio’s yield-to-maturity by averaging each security’s yield in proportion to current par outstanding. It summarizes the market- implied return of the portfolio’s cash flows—under the standard hold-to-maturity assumptions—and is expressed as an annual percentage. It reflects aggregate borrowing costs for the sovereign and the compensation investors demand for holding debt. Use cases Investors can use WAY to compare the income characteristics of various portfolio's and track the historical yields. It can be used alongside weighted average coupon to understand a better picture about the income characteristics of portfolio. Tracking the time series of yields for portfolio against Fed Funds provides a continuously updated snapshot of how much Treasury market has evolved relative to policy rate. records.text: Inflation risks have subsided somewhat given the energy relief following the US-Iran deal, but in their place the market has repriced US front-end rates following the hawkish FOMC messaging. As markets adapt to a shift in Fed communication, we expect greater policy uncertainty to support vol and see scope for greater reactivity to individual datapoints and Fed communication. Our forecasts and longer-term valuations argue for a steepening bias in the US, but with hawkish risks boosting front-end yields and compressing long-end risk premium, we think positioning for belly outperformance on the curve offers the best near-term risk/reward for longs. Energy relief narrows the outcomes for European rates, favouring lower vol and EGB carry, but we think the prospects for much lower yields are limited. In contrast, we expect more macro relief for front-end UK rates as the BoE remains on hold and energy inflation subsides. We favour 2s10s GBP steepeners as fiscal risk premium remains elevated following the Makerfield by-election. With the BoJ having delivered a hike without more hawkish guidance on the path or end-point of the tightening cycle, fiscal policy is likely a near-term focal point. We expect the long-end to be more reactive to any developments, but continue to think that risk/reward is more favourable to shorts further in on the curve. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 35 Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Quarterly Forward Yields This section presents implied forward yields derived from the constant maturity curve starting out of end-of-quarter dates. Forward yields indicate the rate available today for investing between two future dates, inferred from the shape of the yield curve. They translate spot rates into forward-looking expectations of returns, providing insight into anticipated policy trajectories and term premium structure across maturities. Use cases Strategists use forward yields starting out of end-of-quarter dates to properly compare quarterly forecasts to the appropriate market forwards. Portfolio managers use them to better assess the meaning of consensus quarterly forecasts. Risk managers running scenario stress tests with quarterly projections use them to compare bond yield scenarios to market-implied forward yields. In cable, copper is used in low- voltage power and power distribution systems. Non-cable applications include other power distribution functions, cooling systems and network equipment, including server racks, busbars, busways and switchgear . The US and China dominate the build out of hyperscale data centres, accounting for about 40–50% and 16–27% of installed capacity respectively. US facilities are typically built as large campus-style developments operating independently, while Chinese facilities tend to be interconnected clusters of data centres. These regional differences in infrastructure (and power capacity) result in some disparity in the required copper intensity per facility. In that context, we expect the FOMC to hold rates instead of hiking them. Given the signals it sent today, we expect the committee to favor a hold until it is very confident that inflation is returning to its 2% target, that is not before 2028. However, as we described in What would trigger a 2026 Fed hike?, we continue to see risks around this baseline rate path as tilted toward the upside, with possible rate hikes if longer-run inflation expectations were to rise persistently, inflation were to settle at or above 2.5%, well above the Fed's target, with little prospect of declining, or if economic activity and the labor market would show signs of sustained reacceleration. Beyond 2027, we continue to view the longer-run neutral rate as close to or slightly below the current level, at 3.25-3.50%. Which measure of carry is worth following? This will depend on inflation outturns which in turn will also be informed by energy prices. Nominal measures of carry out- perform once inflation has peaked and starts declining, but real measures of carry perform better if inflation is firming. So if energy prices decline, look for returns to rotate towards currencies with high nominal carry. Preferred high yielding candidates are AUD and NOK in DM and ZAR, MXN, HUF and INR in EM. records.text: e The door is kept open to modest hikes with the MPC noting that risks to energy prices remain on the upside (due to logistical delays/instability), inflation pressures are already in the pipeline and MPC is alert to the risk of elevated oil prices for a longer period. Bailey noted that he will respond promptly to any signal that an extended period of high energy prices could be leading to stronger possible second round effects and that risks to inflation/rates are on the upside. So far evidence on second round effects is mixed- business own price expectations have fallen, while household inflation expectations may have become more sensitive to near term inflation news. But the tone was cautious and suggests they are in no hurry to act, if at all. The Iran- US deal has lowered energy prices and so far, inflation/growth impact has been as expected. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 49 Government Bonds | Weighted-Average Coupon Weighted-average coupon (WAC) measures a portfolio's stated income rate by averaging each security's coupon in proportion to current par outstanding. It summarizes the coupon profile and is expressed in annual percentage, providing an aggregate view of the portfolio's income characteristics. Use cases Investors can use WAC to compare the income characteristics of various portfolio's and track the historical trends in the coupon issuance. Strategists can use this in conjunction with the total amount of that portfolio to check on the flows of coupon to be coming into the market. Using WAC along with weighted-average yield (WAY) and weighted average maturity (WAM) depicts a better picture about the portfolio's income characteristics. Calculation methodology We calculate a portfolio's weighted-average coupon by multiplying each bonds's coupon by its weight in the portfolio. The weighting is done based on the par amount held in the portfolio. We then sum the weighted coupon to produce the weighted-average coupon of sovereign portfolio. records.text: 6 Euro Area Viewpoint | 18 June 2026 What’s the ECB call at the moment? The ECB hiked its deposit rate to 2.25% in the June meeting. Its approach here is one of “risk management” and a supposedly “holistic view” of inflation (ECB buzz words in bold italics). We expect one more hike in July, although Iran peace deal news and the drop in the oil price have increased the risk of a delay to September and perhaps even the risk of no further hike from here. Hiking faster and more forcefully than peers (notably the Fed or the BoE) when the economy is weaker and core inflation lower is arguably not only a function of the ECB’s inflation mandate but also reflects the central bank’s lower tolerance for above-target spot inflation and upside risks to the medium term. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 18 June 2026 5 Quantitative Tightening (QT) – i.e., the rolling-off of previous asset purchases from the central banks’ balance sheet via lack of reinvestment on maturity – is on auto-pilot. The ECB is in an especially challenging spot: the Euro area has one monetary policy, but different economic or fiscal policies and a set of fiscal rules too tight for purpose. During big economic shocks, that often leaves the ECB as the biggest and most forceful Euro area-wide decision-maker. The lack of policy mix coordination in the Euro area has tended to overburden monetary policy to support the economy. Can the ECB really diverge from the Fed? Every time we have diverging forecasts from the ECB and the Fed, we are asked the same question: can the ECB hike (or cut) when the Fed doesn’t? Our answer remains that, yes, the ECB can and has in the past. In the end, both central banks have a mandate geared to their respective economies. If fundamentals diverge, monetary policy will too. As a consequence, we take the potential for changes in central bank policy rate differentials very seriously. A related question is, of course, does the exchange rate matter? The ECB answer to this would typically be: “we do not target the exchange rate”. However, in practice, there have been attempts to influence the exchange rate. records.text: 8 Sources: CRU, BNP Paribas Fig. 14: Aluminium substitution is marginal in datacentres, with its share rising by just 3pp between 2025–2030 Sources: CRU forecasts, BNP Paribas 18/06/2026 Copper intensity to plateau; fibre substitution more likely than aluminium METAL Copper still the preferred metal: While aluminium is used in data centres, we see it as a complement to copper rather than a meaningful substitute . Aluminium tends to be deployed in lower-density infrastructure such as the medium and ultra-high- voltage distribution cables connecting the data centre to the substation transformer, where its low weight and cost advantages outweigh the use of copper. Beyond that, substitution is marginal. At high-density nodes – where reliability, efficiency and heat tolerance matter most – copper remains the metal of choice. Its performance cannot be matched by aluminium in these critical sections, as aluminium conducts only about-60% as well as copper. Consequently, the copper–aluminium mix is segmented: aluminium handles peripheral, low-density links, while copper dominates the core infrastructure, leaving little room for direct competition . Fibre optics adoption: We believe the key substitution threat to copper comes in the form of fibre optics. Although the upfront cost is higher, it provides much higher bandwidth, faster speeds and a longer service life. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 69 Government Bonds | Weekly Issuance | Gross DV01 This measure calculates the gross DV01 created by new government bond issuance each week. DV01 represents the change in value for a one-basis-point shift in yields. By aggregating across auctions, the metric quantifies how much new issuance contributes to total market interest rate risk before considering maturities or redemptions rolling off the sovereign debt stock. Use cases Investors use gross DV01 to assess the scale of new supply and its potential to pressure yields. Dealers monitor it to anticipate balance sheet impacts from absorbing issuance. Strategists track it to evaluate short-term shifts in rate sensitivity from Treasury supply. Risk managers incorporate it into models to measure systemic risk from increased bond issuance. Calculation methodology We calculate DV01 for each new issue using modified duration and auction size. We aggregate across all securities issued in the week to compute gross DV01. This measure quantifies the additional systemic interest rate sensitivity introduced by supply, independent of coupons and maturities rolling off. The methodology follows sovereign issuance analysis frameworks. The uploaded values are in US dollar terms by default, however, a toggle allows users to use it in local currency terms. To date, though, we see little evidence that software inflation in the CPI is unusually high, possibly with the exception of a brief spike early last year. In theory, price indexes should measure changes in the cost of a fixed quality item, so that charging for product improve- ments does not mechanically produce inflation. In the CPI for software, this has been accomplished via the matched-model approach. With this method, the BLS does not try to explicit- ly measure quality changes in new software versions. Instead, as each new version of a package is introduced, the BLS observes how the price on the older versions falls. The matched-model approach becomes more challenging if software switches to a subscription model, in which new fea- tures are introduced continuously and no older version of the software is offered for sale. This alone could bias up software prices. The problem is then compounded if the addition of new AI features raises prices. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 51 Government Bonds | DV01 Risk DV01 risk measures the risk of holding bonds in a portfolio for one-basis point move in yields. The measure reflects the sensitivity of the debt portfolio to the parallel shifts in the interest rates curve. Use cases Portfolio managers use DV01 to compare rate sensitivity across securities, strategies, and portfolios. At the portfolio level, it helps assess aggregate duration risk, estimate potential gains or losses under parallel yield-curve shifts, and monitor how interest-rate exposure evolves through time. DV01 can also be used to measure how much risk is entering the market and how that risk is distributed across investor segments. For example, it can help assess the share of market DV01 absorbed by the Federal Reserve versus the private sector, providing a useful lens on supply, demand, and risk-bearing capacity in the rates market—a particularly useful measure for tracking QE/QT. Calculation methodology We compute the portfolio DV01 by summing the individual DV01s of all bonds, as DV01 is an additive measure. For each bond, DV01 is derived by estimating how its price would change if the entire yield curve moves up or down by one basis point. In simple terms, it captures a bond’s price sensitivity to small yield movements. A higher DV01 indicates that the portfolio’s market value is more sensitive to small yield movements. An emerging switch is especially evident in China, where multimode fibre is increasingly favoured for high-speed interconnections. Fibre primarily replaces copper used in communications rather than power infrastructure, but we still think its increasing penetration may contribute to a gradual decline in overall copper intensity. Power distribution efficiency: We expect efficiency gains to gradually reduce the amount of copper required in data centres with emerging advances in power infrastructure perhaps the most compelling example. This is evidenced by a gradual shift towards higher-voltage power distribution which has seen the long-standing 480VAC standard replaced in many data centres by 800VDC. Because a higher voltage can transmit the same power with a lower current and thinner conductors, this cuts the amount of copper required while also reducing power losses. We believe this transition will be a key driver for declining copper intensity. Reaching a plateau: The rollout of fibre optics together with the current headwinds in data centre construction should push copper intensity downward, in our view, after which we expect it to flatten into a long-term plateau. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 79 Government Bonds | Size of the Basis Trade These tickers provide a way to estimate the size of the basis trade in the Treasury cash space. Given its role in previous episodes of stress, many market participants want to be able to track it for signs of stress. The size is constructed split out by contract type and translated into the size of the bonds side of the trade. Use cases Due to the basis trade's role in the 2020 Treasury market's episode of illiquidity, monitoring the size of the trade for stretched or extreme positioning is important both for end users of Treasury futures, as well as regulators. These measures can be used to guard against future episodes of stress and note patterns in this important trade. Calculation methodology To estimate the size of the basis trade, we augment data from the CFTC's Commitments of Traders report. To filter out directional shorts and include parties besides traditional hedge funds who can hold basis positions, we aggregate the net short positions of leveraged funds and dealers by UST future contract. We then perform an adjustment by the conversion factor to better size the basis trade in cash bond space.
