Monetary policy accounts; quarterly ECB forecasts

records.text: with the ECB President and the Vice President. The ECB also releases “monetary policy accounts” – i.e., meeting minutes, released four weeks after the meeting. Unlike elsewhere, this is not a proper “protocol” but a heavily edited (and very long) document. As such, it can also provide hints on the ECB view on developments after the policy meeting. How does the ECB make forecasts? It is worth keeping in mind the following elements in quarterly ECB forecasts: • The cut-off date for forecasts is usually three weeks ahead of the relevant policy meeting. Energy price assumptions are based on the 10-day average of futures until cut-off. Interest rate assumptions (3m Euribor, 10-year sovereign yields) are based on 10-day average forwards. Exchange rates (EURUSD and the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate, NEER) are assumed constant at the 10-day average at cut-off. • Policy assumptions: the ECB doesn’t project a monetary policy path itself; rather, it embeds market expectations of the path in its forecasts (via the 3m Euribor curve). Fiscal policy measures are only included once they have passed relevant legislation. • Forecasts are extended by one calendar year (to three years ahead) each December. • March and September forecasts are conducted “top down” by ECB staff, while June and December ones are a bottom-up exercise with country-specific forecasts by the relevant national central banks. Calculation methodology We model EM currency returns as a function of key global risk factors, including broad dollar strength, global interest rates, and measures of risk appetite. For each currency, we estimate sensitivities to these common drivers using a rolling regression framework. The fitted component represents the portion of FX returns explained by global factors, while the residual captures the idiosyncratic return component. We then standardize this residual using a rolling window to express the series in z-score terms, producing a normalized measure of idiosyncratic risk premium that is comparable across currencies and through time (see Assessing Risk Premia in EMFX (Part 1): A Two- Factor Model Approach). records.text: Ben Luk 18 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Finally , a Turning Point for Asia Risk assets have rallied over the past week, supported by World Cup fever alongside the US-Iran peace deal, with EM FX, equities, and bonds strengthening as the USD extended its decline. However, real money sentiment towards EM remains deeply negative, with 5-day, 10 -day, and 20 -day flows still tracking near bottom-quartile leve ls, highlighting a disconnect between price action and flows. Asia stands to benefit disproportionately from the easing in geopolitical tensions. Having been the worst-performing EM sub-region since the onset of the Middle East conflict, the reopening of the Strait and resulting alleviation of supply side shocks should lower energy costs, ease inflation pressures, and reduce the need for aggressive central bank tightening. This is likely to translate into an improvement in terms of trade and a gradual recovery in capital flows, given Asia’s sensitivity to oil dynamics . We have closed our long CNH/INR but retained our long TWD/IDR on continued idiosyncratic fundamental divergence. We also initiate a short USD/KRW, given KRW’s high beta to a weaker USD backdrop and its leverage to the ongoing rebound in risk sentiment. records.text: t consensus over what actually constitutes data-centre demand. Reports on copper intensity range from as little as 5t/MW to as much as 47t/MW. This large disparity reflects a number of factors: ▪ Apples and oranges: Traditional data centres typically operate at roughly a 5– 30MW capacity whereas a hyperscale AI data centre can reach several hundred MW. Higher capacity results in significantly higher power and cooling infrastructure requirements – and therefore a larger copper requirement per MW. ▪ Where to draw the line? Boundary definitions differ materially across datasets. Lower estimates tend to capture copper contained only within the data centre itself, while higher estimates incorporate other infrastructure, including additional copper used inside the grid. ▪ Double counting: When accounting for material both in the data centre and the grid, tonnage numbers appear frequently inflated. Substation transformers are often counted as part of the grid and then counted again as part of the datacentre. ▪ Regional design differences: Grid architecture and facility design differ depending on their location, contributing to variations in estimated copper intensity per MW. In the absence of consistent layouts and boundaries, intensity is therefore not directly comparable across regions. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 19 June 2026 7 Mann could back a hike in upcoming meeting, but rest would need more to shift Mann’s paragraph suggests that she could go for an activist hike, even in a rapid resolution scenario. For today she noted that she has time to wait as forceful action can have a big impact on inflation expectations. Lombardelli noted that signals that inflation could persist above target would require a response. Ramsden puts equal weight to Scenario A and B and notes that second round effect may be limited, absent further escalation. Breeden notes that chance of material second round effects is small but will act early if they become likely. Dhingra is open to hikes if situation were to worsen. Our call for hikes in July and Sept is subject to risks Overall, the door is open to hikes if the energy price shock is prolonged or second round effects show up. But the reaction function seems to suggest that if the fall is energy prices is sustained and second round effects remain limited, then risks of a look through from the BoE is likely to rise. Our call for hikes in July and September is subject to risks. The peace deal, dovish data and BoE’s caution have increased risks of one delayed or no hike at all. We plan to review our BoE call shortly.

records.text: suggest hyperscalers are becoming more selective in new project commitments, amid tighter access to power, grid bottlenecks and longer equipment lead times (see US data centers power demand: Supply, Infrastructure to hamper growth, dated 20 January, and pages 11–14). However, given the robust growth in live and under- construction capacity, we think it is likely more a reflection of pipeline rationalisation than evidence of a broader slowdown in AI-driven data-centre demand . Virginia and Texas are still the two largest US markets, accounting for around 20% and 15% of US headline capacity respectively (Figure 6), and exceeding most national markets. Both have seen strong growth: Virginia‘s live capacity reached 6.8GW at end-2025 (+16% y/y), with 3.8GW under construction (+40%); Texas’s live capacity reached 4.2GW (+30%), with 2.5GW under construction (+83%). Beyond FLAP-D: Europe’s data-centre market has been anchored in the so-called ‘FLAP-D’ hubs (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin), supported by early compute demand and established fibre networks. We still expect investment into these markets, but think grid constraints, elevated power prices, limited land availability and regulatory hurdles will weigh on new development – and we note demand is already spilling over into alternative European growth markets, including the Nordics and Spain (Figure 4). records.chunk_id: Data_centres_update_H2_2026_New_hotspots_old_constraints_Desknote--926569.pdf-11-29
records.text: get near the 2013–2021 average (Figure 21, page 12) and are a long way off the 5,000 miles of annual additions implied as necessary in a Department of Energy 2024 report, according to one estimate (Grid Strategies, July 2025). We see some positive momentum in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission commitment to act by end-June on a DoE proposal to standardise the process for very large electricity users to connect to the interstate transmission grid. The proposal aims to prioritise on-site generation, standardise new and hybrid large loads, and reduce project review timelines. We note that the effectiveness of the measures will depend on how much survives the legislative process . Physical shortages of grid equipment remain a key bottleneck. Surging demand has pushed power wire and cable costs to nearly triple their 2018 level, while transformer and switchgear prices have roughly doubled (Figure 23). The lead time for key grid components is now around 3–5 years (Figure 24). It doesn’t help that the US relies heavily on imports – domestic production meets only 20% of large power transformer demand and 50% of distribution transformer demand, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even if domestic manufacturing scales up, it will take time to come online and will still depend on key components from other countries. We therefore think grid-equipment deficits will continue to constrain power-system growth in the US through 2030. 18/06/2026 No easing in supply constraints US POWER Forecast

After broadly stagnating from 2015 to 2019, the rise has resumed in the post-COVID recovery, and reached a high point in 2024 (close to 16%). Much of that increase was driven by increased shipments of moderate and high complexity products, a factor arguably making Chinese products less substitutable. The increase in Chinese market share is particularly pronounced in textiles, machinery and transportation, markets in which the both geographies compete. • We assess economic complexity using the Product Complexity Index (PCI) from the Observatory of Economic Complexity. This metric reflects the knowledge and sophistication required to produce an item, considering factors such as the diversity of a country's exports, the capabilities of its industries and their geographic concentration. Based on this index, we define four tiers: very low complexity items are those with a PCI score lower than -0.85; low complexity items have a PCI between -0.85 and zero; moderate complexity items are associated with a PCI between zero and 0.85; and highly complex items have a PCI score above that value. • Recent monthly export data indicate a sizable acceleration of Chinese exports since the end of 2025, with shipments accelerating by close to 20% y/y in May, largely on the back on strong AI-related international demand. records.Author: Abiel Reinhart

Catalyst.Metric: Core CPI; Core PCE; DRAM; NAND flash prices

records.text: tion • Adding AI features to subscription software could raise measured prices, though we see little of that yet AI may raise near-term inflation via three main channels. First, DRAM and NAND flash computer memory have surged in price because of higher demand from data centers and a supply shift toward high bandwidth memory, with some older storage technologies also now seeing price increases. Second, the introduction of new AI features in software could raise measured prices. Third, data center investment may raise retail electricity prices. We discuss the first two factors in this note, and conclude that higher prices for hardware are the main source of inflation pressure, though the software angle bears watching. Each 10% increase in hardware costs would raise core CPI and PCE inflation around 0.1%, and we estimate a 0.2-0.4% lift to inflation given the shock to memo- ry prices, with some of this having already occurred. Semiconductor weights in the CPI and PCE While semiconductors are used in a range of devices, we focus on key products, including computers and peripherals, tablets, smartphones, smartwatches, video game consoles, and smart home assistants. We estimate that prior to the current spike in tech prices these items accounted for about 0.9% of the core CPI and 1.1% of the core PCE (Table 1). Conversely, share buybacks fell short, totaling Rmb0.4tn (-11% yoy). This decline in n buybacks was heavily concentrated in Internet (Retailing and Media), where buyback volume fell 28% in 2025 as companies prioritized AI spending and quick commerce subsidies. Despite lower volumes, net buybacks remain accretive to EPS for existing MSCI China universe (ex-Financials). Shifts in corporate cash allocation: Beyond shareholder returns, growth n investments grew by 3% yoy (vs. -5% in 2024). Sector-level spending varied dramatically underneath a flat Capex (remaining at Rmb6.4tn): Retailing, Tech Hardware, and Media grew by 94%, 22%, and 16% yoy, respectively, whereas Real Estate, Solar Equipment, and Materials declined by 33%, 48%, and 8% yoy, reflecting a disciplined approach to capacity expansion in oversupplied industries. Outlook for June: Headline -0.3pp to 2.9%, core -0.2pp to 2.4% Following four consecutive monthly increases, we forecast headline inflation to decline by 0.3pp to 2.9% y/y in June. With energy prices falling further, we expect a 2.5pp drop in energy inflation (to 8.3% y/y) to be the main driver of the decline. As volatile and seasonal services drove the pickup in core inflation in May, we expect the unwinding of these components to lead to a 0.2pp fall in core to 2.4%. At the sub-component level, services inflation is projected to decline by 0.3pp to 3.2% y/y, while goods inflation is expected to remain unchanged at 0.9% y/y. Following an unexpected 0.5pp drop in May, food inflation is likely to edge up by 0.1pp to 2.0% in June. Looking ahead, while we think headline inflation likely peaked at 3.2% in May, we expect food and goods inflation to pick up towards year-end as higher input costs (particularly energy and fertiliser) are gradually passed through to consumers. (These are the so-called "indirect effects" of the first round effects). Importantly, we do not anticipate a reacceleration in services inflation, consistent with our view that second-round effects will be more limited than during the 2022 energy shock. Heightened reactivity will likely translate into higher US rates vol, in turn supporting USD–pair FX vol, in our view. Across major USD–FX pairs, AUDUSD, EURUSD, and GBPUSD exhibit high correlation with US rates vol. Of these pairs, GBPUSD vol has historically been one of the most sensitive to US inflation uncertainty. As with many other FX pairs, GBPUSD implied vol is low and reflects little risk premium ; the gap between 6m implied and WMR realised is near zero (Figure 3). Our MarFA™ analysis signals that GBPUSD implied vol is low (Figure 4), considering the current macro backdrop. We favour vol swaps, as their strikeless nature means they are long atm-gamma around event risks, a feature that could be valuable in this environment. Low level of implied vol and low surface risk premium mean vol swaps trade near implieds and close to the cycle low of realised vol in GBPUSD, reducing ex-ante risk on such a structure. We add a cap to the vol swap to further improve entry levels, noting that 6m realised vol has typically remained below 10% over the last few years. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 37 Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Carry & Roll Down Roll down and carry tickers provide a clear decomposition of expected returns under a stable yield curve. Roll down isolates the effect of curve-driven yield movements, while carry captures income and financing effects over the holding period. Together, they provide a systematic framework for understanding structural return opportunities embedded in fixed-income portfolios. Use cases Investors use carry and roll down to identify tenors offering higher risk-adjusted returns under a stable yield curve. Segments with stronger carry and roll down indicate maturities that may outperform through time decay and yield convergence. This supports relative value analysis and highlights attractive curve positions. In strategy design, these measures guide curve trades such as steepeners and flatteners by quantifying expected returns driven by time and curve effects. Calculation methodology We first construct the par curve using the methodology outlined in the Government Bonds | Constant Maturity | Par/Spot Yields. Roll down measures the change in yield that arises purely from the passage of time, assuming the yield curve’s shape remains unchanged. It illustrates how a bond’s yield would evolve as it rolls down the curve toward shorter maturities under a stable curve assumption. In the fourth quarter of last year, industrial metals looked poised to extend their breakout rally following a couple of years of rangebound price action. Precious metals appeared to be in a well-entrenched bull market, which, combined with the broader com- modity price trends, pointed to an ongoing debasement regime. Finally, the Treasury market was bullishly ranging in the richer end of its multi-year trading range. While that last factor could have sent the dollar in either direction, the front-end rally had not yet broken through multi-year pattern resistance to drive a flight-to-quality flow into the dollar. Combined with the metals-driven debasement trend, that cross-market setup didn’t match typical historical bullish dollar regimes. Fast forward six months and the industrial metals rally has decelerated materially after hit- ting the upper end of the target zone we envisioned as we wrote our bullish outlook for 1H26 back in November. The market is also roughly priced for a global manufacturing PMI near 53 on a simple regression model, slightly above the current data and at its highest level in a few years. KEY MESSAGES We cut our 2026 GDP growth forecast for Chile to 1.6% (from 2.4%) due to a sharp Q1 slowdown and export weakness, but a robust private-investment pipeline should support a rebound to 3.0% growth in 2027. Considering the downside surprise in May inflation, we lower our 2026 year-end inflation forecast to 4.0% (from 4.2%), and expect a gradual move towards the Chilean central bank’s 3% target for 2027. Given the softer inflation, weaker GDP growth and external uncertainties, we expect BCCh to maintain a ‘meeting by meeting’ approach and keep the policy rate at 4.5% for an extended period. We now see a structural fiscal deficit of 2.5% of GDP, driven by lower revenues, higher energy spending and an extra USD6.2bn funding need. Meanwhile, opposition in the Senate may delay the full implementation of President Kast’s tax-cut and pension reforms until after 2028. Strategy: The latest BCCh monetary-policy report signals near-term rates stability, making US Treasury yields the main driver of Chilean yields, in our view, and postponing our re-entry into Camara payers. The statement noted that another hike will be delivered if required, a reminder that will, in our view, be maintained in upcoming meetings given that annual inflation will remain high, requiring some pushback against pricing which now implies only a slight hiking bias (+15bp to terminal). Still, plugging our expectation for the data into the now more data-dependent reaction function, it does seem likely that the hiking cycle is done. Next week’s May CPI report, for example, should consolidate that 2Q is tracking below SoMP forecasts. We maintain the AUD-USD 2Y1Y (IRS-SFR) spread tightener entered in early May, in part acknowledging the evolving Fed outlook. The case can be made for adding further domestic bullish proxies, but the broader context is important, as with global growth risks tilting upward, and the RBA having moved ahead of the Fed, cross-market steepeners appear a better expression than outright longs. This was reiterated at their June meeting where they noted higher interest rates faced by households and business remain higher, which will act to reduce inflation over time. So without moving policy rates, they have influenced both front-end pricing and contained inflation expectations. Five-year, five-year inflation swaps are now back to where they were at the end of February, when short-rate markets were still discounting cuts, not hikes. The message: like Maradona, the BoE can get to goal without needing to move. The challenge is that the BoE is not the only potentially consequential policy shift this week. Assuming Andy Burnham is elected to Parliament on Thursday, a challenge to Keir Starmer’s premiership and Labour leadership looks increasingly likely. Prediction markets have flagged that risk for months, but with the probability now close to 90%, asset managers appear to be acting. Hike premium is likely removed only slowly, essentially one meeting at a time. Indeed, the minutes noted the “full and fast pass-through” of higher rates was “already acting to reduce inflation”. In other words, the effective tightening via the market is doing the work without the need for the BoE to hike. Growing hawkish dissent, but it carries less weight. As money market rates increase, banks may also find it increasingly advantageous to make use of the ECB’s open market operations (OMOs). There is a potential stigma associated with using the ECB’s OMO, which may partly hinder the initial uptake, but the more advantageous pricing appears relative to market rates, the less significant the stigma would likely be. The two main OMOs currently available are the main refinancing operation (MRO) and longer-term refinancing operation (LTRO) – see Exhibit 12. The MRO rate is equal to the ECB’s depo rate + 15bp (currently equivalent to c. €STR + 22bp). Looking ahead, new structural operations are on the horizon If OMO usage increases meaningfully, the ECB has communicated a desire to eventually introduce structural operations, starting with longer-term refinancing operations, which would act as an alternative to the then assumed material usage of MRO and LTRO. This would be expected to be followed by a structural securities portfolio. Information is limited so far, and we look for further details as we progress in 2026 and into 2027.

records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 41 Government Bonds | TIPS Breakevens Carry These measures provide carry estimates for on-the-run Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) and matched-maturity TIPS breakeven positions across standard holding horizons. Carry for a bond is the return earned from holding the bond over a specified horizon, assuming the yield curve remains unchanged. This means receiving the coupon payment by holding the bond and subtracting the cost to finance the bond. Use cases Investors use these series to assess the carry benefit or cost of holding TIPS and breakeven positions over 1-month, 3-month, 6-month, and 12-month horizons. They are useful for determining whether TIPS or breakevens are attractive on a carry-adjusted basis, particularly around CPI releases, periods of energy-price volatility, and seasonal inflation windows.They can use breakeven carry to understand how much return comes from seasonal CPI effects versus changes in underlying inflation compensation. Calculation methodology Carry for a bond is the return earned from holding the bond over a specified horizon, assuming the yield curve remains unchanged. This means receiving the coupon payment by holding the bond and subtracting the cost to finance the bond. We compute the bonds forward pricing using the Proceeds Method. records.text: 10 Euro Area Viewpoint | 18 June 2026 Monitoring the balance sheet and reserve demand ECB balance sheet data is observable on a weekly basis on the ECB’s website1. The different items on the asset and liability side can also be monitored on Bloomberg, by going to the ECB’s page (ECB <Go>) and then clicking on the left item “Financial Statement”. The ECB also provides monthly QT volumes for 2026 and 2027 split both by asset type and domicile of issuer for maturing security, which helps make projections for the evolution of its balance sheet size 2 – see also our latest ECB Balance Sheet update report. While there are no standard tradeable contracts that are priced by the size of the Eurosystem balance sheet, it is a key factor in various money market rates. First, as reserve scarcity increases, market borrowing can re-price higher, which generally results in the €STR- ECB depo spread increasing. Second, in addition to €STR, there are various other EUR benchmarks used for interest rate swaps whose fixings are not derived by overnight funding but instead derived by fixings on term funding basis. These include 1- week, 1-month, 3-month, 6-month and 12-month Euribor rates. As Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) regulation favours term funding vs overnight, Euribor fixings have the potential to deviate from €STR when market funding demand increases (Exhibit 11). records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 15 Market-Implied | # of Months to Peak/Trough Policy Rates This indicator estimates how many months forward markets imply central banks will take to reach terminal policy rates, either at the peak of tightening or the trough of easing. Use cases The primary use case of this ticker is to indicate the number of months until the peak or trough policy rate is reached. In effect, it provides a market-implied time line of how long the current policy regime is expected to last by the central banks. Calculation methodology We first identify the peak and trough of the curve using the methodology mentioned in the Market-Implied | Peak/Trough Central Bank Policy Rates. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 18 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General UK policy makers look back to Maradona Just as the Fed moves to a data driven more reactive approach, UK policy makers are heading back to the Estadio Azteca and the Maradona theory of economic policy. But which goal from that infamous game between England and Argentina in June 1986 is the right model? Can the mere anticipation of policy movements really do the job or will markets just need to take the punches? Former BoE Governor and avid soccer fan Mervyn King introduced the Maradona theory of monetary policy more than 20 years ago. His analogy was Maradona’s second goal against England in 1986: he beat five defenders while running almost in a straight line because each expected him to move and reacted accordingly. King’s point was that central banks could do something similar. Clear communication, or forward guidance, can move expectations without the need to move rates. And that, more or less, has been the story of 2026 so far. In response to February’s inflation shock, our metrics show the BoE’s tone shifted dramatically, taking rate expectations with it (Figure 1). That anticipated tightening was enough to keep longer-run inflation expectations contained, certainly compared with the 2021/22 transitory inflation debacle (Figure 2). records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 21 Proxy Effective Federal Funds Rate The proxy rate summarizes the stance of monetary policy on and off the zero lower bound (ZLB) by inferring from the common movement of government and private sector interest rates. It tracks the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) in normal times and extends into negative territory at the ZLB, providing a continuous, market-implied gauge of policy stance. Use cases The primary use case is to estimate the Federal Reserve’s policy stance during the zero lower bound (ZLB). By drawing on rates across asset classes, it provides a single, continuous measure that reflects broader financial conditions, not just Treasury yields. Investors can also use it to judge whether the effective stance feels tighter or looser than the headline policy rate implies. Beyond the ZLB, it remains valuable for identifying periods when financial conditions tighten or loosen ahead of formal rate changes, as observed in 2022 when the proxy rate rose well before the first FOMC hike. It can be substituted for the effective fed funds rate in standard macro models to produce regime- invariant estimates of monetary policy shocks and their transmission to output, inflation, and employment, eliminating the structural break the ZLB otherwise introduces. records.text: M Global Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 91 Foreign Exchange Implied Volatility Index The Foreign Exchange Implied Volatility Index is a model-free gauge of expected currency market volatility, constructed as the weighted average of three-month at-the-money implied volatilities across the most liquid G10 and emerging-market FX pairs. Designed as the FX analogue of the equity VIX, it condenses global option prices into a single measure of forward-looking FX uncertainty. Use cases Investors use the index to benchmark global FX risk in the same way they use the VIX for equity markets. Rising index levels signal higher expected volatility and potential stress across currencies. Portfolio managers employ it in carry trade risk management, hedging cost estimation, and portfolio stress testing, while strategists use it to track shifts in macro risk sentiment. Calculation methodology We source 3M at-the-money implied volatilities from FX option markets for the most traded G10 and EM pairs. Each volatility is weighted by liquidity, reflecting trading volume and open interest. We then average across pairs using a geometric aggregation to produce a single index. The procedure mirrors the construction principles of the VIX, adapted to FX markets. What are we watching for in the coming months? One, any evidence of indirect effects via food and core goods inflation in the coming inflation prints. We will also be watching closely inflation expectations, firms' own price expectations, and future wage growth as part of the July DMP survey. Figure 1: Rangy FX Markets Figure 2: Volume (5-day, percentiles) Weekly Insights: A hawkish Fed and a renewed push higher in the US dollar might bring long - awaited range breaks. FX markets are historically somnolent, nowhere more so than in JPY crosses The average width of ranges in USDJPY, EURJPY, GBPJPY and AUDJPY over the last month has narrowed to 1.7%, a 0.3% percentile reading over a 20 year history, only 30bps greater than the narrowest ranges on record. For comparison, the range in the similarly sleepy DXY is 2.4%, which at least gets it out of the bottom quartile while still offering little e xcitement. Trend followers would surely love to see this break out even further. Volume: Activity in the market has never been all that suppressed this year, despite it mostly being a low volatility period. Volumes are holding above median in both DM and EM blocs. Most EM pairs save USDSGD saw higher interest and DM Commodity pairs remain robustly traded. Depth of Book: Liquidity conditions look healthy but our metrics for G10 and EM FX aggregates dropped out of the top quartile last week. The biggest surprise came from the Fed which delivered a hawkish dot plot, while Warsh’s first press conference offered little in terms of guidance. The BoE and Riksbank showed little urgency to act, we have pushed back our call for a hike to November and December respectively. The revisions to the Norges Bank rate path were modestly hawkish, we still call for a September hike but with risks of an earlier move. The RBA paused at 4.35% after three consecutive hikes, we believe they are done for now. • Euro: We maintain bias to trade German duration tactically from long side and look to add OW 10Y Germany on any selloff back to ~3.10%. records.text: 18 June 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 members retained enough optionality to move should second-round effects crystlise more clearly and forcefully, especially with household and firms' inflation expectations still elevated. This, we think, was consistent with the Bank's 'active hold' approach. Maintaining a hawkish bias would allow markets to price in some chance of rate hikes, providing passive tightening of monetary policy should inflationary pressures ramp up – in some way, providing insurance hikes against rising inflation. Moreover, with uncertainty around the medium-term path still elevated, the MPC gave itself as much optionality as possible by retaining the April forward guidance and voicing vigilance around firms' price and wage setting behaviour in the coming months and quarters. Our call: on hold The MPC was given a rare gift over the last week: more time. With data more favourable than expected, and an Iran/US deal in place, the need to act swiftly has reduced. The MPC can let the dust settle before deciding on its next course of action with a full economic update and a more complete communication package in July. We expect Bank Rate to remain on hold through the remainder of the year. We still see the case for rate cuts to resume from spring next year.
